For this reason it is likened in reality to what is uttered by human speech, by the commonality they share in speech. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Bakr, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and al-Aʿmash, with variant transmissions from three of them, read "mithla" in the nominative as an attribute of "laḥaqq." The rest of the seven and the majority read it in the accusative. It was said: it is a fatḥa of indeclinability, and it is an attribute like its state in the reading of one who put it in the nominative. Since it was annexed to a non-declinable word it became indeclinable, and "mā" in this construction is extra for emphasis, and the annexation is to "annakum tanṭiqūn." Al-Māzinī said: "mithl" was built because it was compounded with "mā" and became one word, and similar to it are "waylamā" and "hayyamā" and "ibnamā." Ḥumayd ibn Thawr said:

Surely "hayyamā" for what I have met, and "hayyamā"; and woe to whoever has not met of them the "waylamā."

He said: were it not for the construction it would be nunated. Another poet said:

So honour us, a mother, and honour us, a son (ibnamā).

End of this derivation. "Ibnamā" is not a son built with "mā"; rather this is from the category of adding a mīm to it and following "mā" at the end, since the case-vowel was placed on the mīm. You say: "hādhā ibnam," "ra'aytu ibnamā," "marartu bi-ibnam," and the "mā" in the three cases in "ibnamā" is not compounded with "mā" as he said: the fatḥa in "ibnamā" is a case-vowel, and it is accusative as a specification. The grammarians cited the building of a noun with a particle in the verse of the rajaz:

Is it a bull that I hunt for you, or two bulls, or is it the hornless one with two horns?

It was said: it is an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, its estimate: "innahu la-ḥaqqun ḥaqqan mithla annakum," so its vowel is a case-vowel. It was said: it is accusative as a circumstantial of the pronoun concealed in "laḥaqq," and it was said: a circumstantial of "laḥaqq," though it is indefinite, and al-Jarmī and Sībawayh permitted that in various places of his book. Speech here is an expression for utterance with letters and sounds in the ordering of meanings. People say: "hādhā ḥaqq, as you are here," and "hādhā ḥaqq as you see and hear," and this is like the verse. "Mā" is extra according to the explicit statement of al-Khalīl, and its deletion is not transmitted, so you would not say: "hādhā ḥaqq ka-annaka hāhunā." The Kufans make "mithl" a locus and put it in the accusative as an adverb, and they permit "zaydun mithlaka" with the accusative, so according to their view "mithla" in it may be accusative as an adverb; their argument and the refutation of them is mentioned in grammar. Among the speech of some Bedouins: "Who is it that angered the Friend until he swore?" They did not believe him when he spoke, until they compelled him to the oath.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 51, verse 1–23 (part 1 of 2):

Surat adh-Dhariyat (The Scattering Winds), sixty verses, Meccan.
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)
﴿By the winds that scatter with dispersing,﴾ ﴿and those that bear the burden,﴾ ﴿and those that run with ease,﴾ ﴿and those that distribute by command,﴾ ﴿indeed what you are promised is surely true,﴾ ﴿and indeed the Recompense is surely to occur,﴾ ﴿by the sky with its paths,﴾ ﴿indeed you are in a contradictory saying,﴾ ﴿turned away from it is whoever is turned away,﴾ ﴿destroyed are the liars,﴾ ﴿who are in heedlessness, forgetful,﴾ ﴿they ask, "When is the Day of Recompense?"﴾ ﴿the Day they will be tried over the Fire,﴾ ﴿"Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten."﴾ ﴿Indeed the God-conscious will be in gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿taking what their Lord has given them; indeed they were before that good-doers,﴾ ﴿they used to sleep little of the night,﴾ ﴿and in the hours before dawn they would seek forgiveness,﴾ ﴿and in their wealth was a right for the beggar and the deprived,﴾ ﴿and in the earth are signs for those who are certain,﴾ ﴿and in yourselves; will you not then see?﴾ ﴿and in the sky is your provision and what you are promised,﴾ ﴿so by the Lord of the sky and the earth, indeed it is surely true, just as you speak.﴾ ﴿Has there reached you the story of Abraham's honored guests?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Peace, a people unknown."﴾ ﴿Then he went quickly to his family and brought a fat calf,﴾ ﴿and placed it before them, he said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿So he sensed fear of them; they said, "Do not fear," and gave him glad tidings of a knowing boy,﴾ ﴿Then his wife came forward crying out, and struck her face and said, "A barren old woman!"﴾ ﴿They said, "Thus said your Lord; indeed He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed we have been sent to a criminal people,﴾ ﴿to send upon them stones of clay,﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for the transgressors,﴾ ﴿so We brought out those of the believers who were there,﴾ ﴿but We found there not one house of Muslims,﴾ ﴿and We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment,﴾ ﴿and in Moses, when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority,﴾ ﴿but he turned away with his supporters and said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea, and he was blameworthy,﴾ ﴿and in 'Ad, when We sent upon them the barren wind,﴾ ﴿which left nothing it came upon without making it like crumbled dust,﴾ ﴿and in Thamud, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a while,"﴾ ﴿but they rebelled against the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on,﴾ ﴿and they were not able to stand up, nor were they among those who could defend themselves,﴾ ﴿and the people of Noah before, indeed they were a defiantly disobedient people,﴾ ﴿and the sky We built with power, and indeed We are expanding it,﴾ ﴿and the earth We spread out, and how excellent are the spreaders!﴾ ﴿And of every thing We created pairs, that perhaps you may remember,﴾ ﴿so flee to Allah; indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner,﴾ ﴿and do not set up with Allah another god; indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner.﴾ ﴿Thus no messenger came to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ ﴿Did they charge one another with it? No, they are a transgressing people.﴾ ﴿So turn away from them, and you are not to be blamed,﴾ ﴿and remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers.﴾ ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me,﴾ ﴿I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me.﴾ ﴿Indeed Allah is the Provider, Possessor of strength, the Firm.﴾ ﴿Indeed for those who did wrong is a portion like the portion of their companions, so let them not seek to hasten.﴾ ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved from their Day which they are promised.﴾)
(p-132) Al-hubuk: the paths, like the folds of sand and of still water when the wind strikes it, and likewise the hubuk of hair: the traces of its waviness and crinkling. The poet said:
A poem: "Covered with the roots of the star, woven by a cold wind over the bright surface of its water, hubuk."
The coat of mail is called mahbuka because its rings are fashioned into paths. Its singular is habika, like tariqa and turuq, or hibak like mithal and mithl. The rajaz poet said:
A poem: "As if the weaver had woven it, a carpet with its weft-work hibak."
It is said: hibak is the cord with which the cane-cutter ties his bundle, a long strip made in the arrangement of the rows of planted trees. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "I made the thing firm and did its work well." Al-Farra' said: al-hubuk is the crumpling of everything. Others said: al-mahbuk is the strongly formed one, of a horse or otherwise. Imru' al-Qays said:
A poem: "He has come bearing me on his nose, a swift-stepping, strongly built, firmly made one."
Al-huju': sleep. As-simn: well known, the filling of the body with fat and flesh. It is said: samina, simanan, fa-huwa samin; they departed from the norm in the verbal noun and the active participle, and the analogy would be samina and sammana. They also said: samin, when he has become fat. Adh-dhanub: the great bucket. The rajaz poet said:
A poem: "Indeed, when a stranger attacks us, he has a bucket and we have a bucket, and if you refuse, then we have the well."
Az-Zamakhshari recited it: "For us a bucket, and for you a bucket." It is also used to mean share and portion. 'Alqama ibn 'Abda said:
A poem: "And in every tribe you have spread blessing, so a portion is due to Shas from your generosity."
Az-Zamakhshari attributed it to 'Amr ibn Shas, which is an error in the Diwan of 'Alqama. Al-Harith ibn Abi Shimr al-Ghassani had captured Shas, brother of 'Alqama, so 'Alqama entered to him and praised him with the qasida in which this verse is. When he reached this verse in the recitation, al-Harith said: "Yes, and he has given it." Hassan said:
A poem: "Let Rabi'a ibn Mukarram not be far, and may the morning clouds water his grave with buckets."
Another said:
A poem: "By your life, and the fates are coming, for every son of a father there is a bucket of them."
(p-133) [Quranic text repeated as above]
This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what came before it is that He said: "So remind with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning." At the beginning of this one, after the oath, He said: "Indeed what you are promised is surely true, and indeed the Recompense is surely to occur."
﴿Adh-dhariyat﴾: the winds.
﴿Al-hamilat﴾: the clouds.
﴿Al-jariyat﴾: the ships.
﴿Al-muqassimat﴾: the angels. This is the explanation of 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, from the pulpit, when Ibn al-Kawwa' asked him; it was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas also said: ﴿al-hamilat﴾ are the ships laden with people and their goods. It was said: the carriers are all animals. It was said: al-jariyat are the clouds moved by the winds. It was said: al-jawari are the stars. Abu 'Amr and Hamza assimilated the dhal of ﴿adh-dhariyat﴾ into the dhal of (dharwan), and its scattering is dispersing it for rain or for dust. It was read with a fatha on the waw, naming what is carried by the verbal noun. The meaning of (yusran) is a course with ease, that is, facility. So yusran is a verbal noun described by it with an omitted supposition, so it is in the position of a circumstantial accusative according to Sibawayh's view. (Amran): they distribute affairs of rains, provisions and other things, so amran is the object. It was said: it is a verbal noun in the accusative of circumstance, meaning commanded, and the object of al-muqassimat is omitted. Mujahid said: the affair of the servants is handled by Jibril for harshness, Mika'il for mercy, the Angel of Death for seizing souls, and Israfil for the blowing. About the angels it came: al-muqassimat in the sense of groups. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that the winds alone are meant, because they produce the clouds, carry them, direct them, and move through the air with easy motion, and distribute the rain by the turning of the winds. End of quote. If the referents differ, these are successive divisions. If they do not differ, it is one division, and it is from the conjunction of attributes: they scatter dust and pebbles at the start of their blowing, then they carry the clouds, then run through the air spreading the clouds, then distribute the rain. This is like his saying:
A poem: "Alas for Zayyaba for al-Harith, the one who attacks at dawn, the one who takes booty, the one who returns."
That is: the one who attacked the enemy at dawn, took booty from them, and returned to his people safe and victorious. The sentence sworn to, which is the answer of the oath, is ﴿Indeed what you are promised﴾, and ma is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," with the returning pronoun omitted, that is, you are promised it. It is possible that it is a verbal noun, that is, its promise to you or its threat, since "you are promised" can carry both meanings, being the present of "wa'ada" and the present of "awda'a." It fits being the present of "awda'a" because of His saying: ﴿So remind with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾, and because the intent is intimidation and awe. The meaning of its truth is the certainty of its occurrence, and the one who is truly described as truthful is the one who informs. He said: ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾: that is, one in which truth is found. It was said: (lasadiq), and he placed the active participle in the position of the verbal noun, and there is no need for this supposition. Mujahid said: the more apparent view is that the verse concerns the disbelievers, and that it is pure threat.
﴿And indeed the Recompense﴾: that is, the reward, (lawaqi'): that is, truly issuing upon the responsible ones from mankind and jinn. The apparent meaning of "in the sky" is that it is a collective noun, by which all the heavens are meant. Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As said: it is the seventh heaven. It was said: the cloud that shades the earth.
﴿Dhat al-hubuk﴾: that is, possessing a level, good creation. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Qatada and al-Rabi'. Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿dhat al-hubuk﴾: that is, adorned with stars. Ad-Dahhak said: possessing paths, meaning the Milky Way in the sky. Ibn Zayd said: possessing strength, due to His saying: ﴿seven strong ones﴾ [al-Naba' 12]. It was said: possessing firmness.
The majority read al-hubuk with two dammas. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, with a variant from him, Abu Malik al-Ghifari, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu al-Sammal and Nu'aym from Abu 'Amr read it with a sukun on the ba'. 'Ikrima read it with a fatha, as the plural of habaka, like tarfa and turaf. Abu Malik al-Ghifari and al-Hasan, with a variant from him, read it with a kasra on the ha and ba'. Abu Malik al-Ghifari, al-Hasan also, and Abu Haywa read it with a kasra on the ha and a sukun on the ba', and this is the lightening of fi'il with both kasras, and it is a singular noun, not a plural, because fi'il is not among the patterns of plurals, so it should be counted with ibil among what came as nouns of the pattern fi'il with kasra on the fa and ayn. Ibn 'Abbas also and Abu Malik read it with fatha on both. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: it is the plural of habaka, like 'aqaba and 'aqab. End of quote. Al-Hasan also: al-hibak, with a kasra on the ha and a fatha on the ba'. He also read as the majority did, so his reading became five: al-hubuk, al-hibuk, al-hubk, al-hubak, al-habak. Abu Malik also read: al-hibuk with a kasra on the ha and a damma on the ba', and Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned it from al-Hasan, so he has six readings. The author of al-Lawami', who is unmatched in Arabic in its patterns and measures, said: "I do not know what transmitted it." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is an anomalous reading, not well founded, and it seems he meant the kasra, then imagined "al-hibuk" as the reading with damma after reading the ha with kasra and the ba' with damma, and this is by intermixing of dialects, and this pattern is not found in Arab speech. End of quote.

Thus the grammarians interpreted these readings, but in my view the better reading is that it belongs to those cases where the vowel of the ḥāʾ follows the vowel of dhāt in the kasra, and the unvowelled lām is not taken into account, because a quiescent letter is a weak barrier. The response to the oath is: ﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾. The apparent meaning is that it is a general address to both the believer and the disbeliever, just as the response to the earlier oath includes both of them, and their discord is that some of them are believers in the Messenger (ﷺ) and his Book, and some are disbelievers. Ibn Zayd said: it is an address to the disbelievers, who say: "a sorcerer, a poet, a soothsayer, a madman." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the speech of the disbelievers cannot be consistent; rather it is contradictory and discordant. It was also said: their discord concerns the Resurrection, some of them denying it and some doubting it. It was also said: their discord is their acknowledgement that God Most High brought them into existence, while they worship other than Him, and the sayings they utter about their gods.

(yu'faku): that is, he is turned away from it, that is, from the Qur'an and the Messenger (ﷺ), as said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah.

﴿Whoever is turned away﴾: that is, whoever is turned away with the turning that admits of no greater or more severe turning, in keeping with his saying: "None perishes before God except one who is destined to perish." It was also said: whoever is turned away in the foreknowledge of God Most High, meaning that he is one who is turned away from the truth and does not desist. Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to what you are promised, or to the one who swore by the heaven (p-135) that they are in a discordant saying regarding its occurrence, so some of them are doubtful and some of them are deniers. Then he said: "is turned away from belief in the matter of the Resurrection is the one who is turned away." It was also said: the one turned away from is omitted, and ʿan here denotes cause, and the pronoun refers to ﴿a discordant saying﴾, meaning that by means of it is turned away whoever wishes to embrace Islam, by saying: "It is sorcery; it is soothsaying." This was related by al-Zahrāwī and al-Zamakhsharī, and he presented it, in his customary manner of presenting what is reported from others as his own invention. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: It is possible that it refers to ﴿a discordant saying﴾, and the meaning is: whoever has his happiness prevail is turned away from it by God's granting of success into Islam; and this is on the basis that it is a discordant saying of the disbelievers, except that the usage of the idiom in its falsehood is turning from good to evil, and therefore you find it only in those who are blamed. End, and there is some abridgement in it. Ibn Jubayr and Qatādah read: "man afaka," with the active voice, meaning: whoever the people have turned away from it, and they are the Quraysh. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read: "ya'fiku ʿanhu man afaka," meaning: whoever is himself turned away turns people away from it. Also from him: "ya'fiku ʿanhu man afaka," meaning: whoever is a great liar turns people away from it. And it was read: "yu'fanu ʿanhu man afana," with nūn in both, meaning: whoever is deprived is deprived of it, from afana al-ḍarʿ, when he milked it to exhaustion.

﴿Killed be the conjecturers﴾: that is, God has destroyed the conjecturers, who are those who estimate what is not valid.

﴿In a heedless state﴾: in ignorance that overwhelms them. (heedless): unmindful of what they were commanded.

﴿They ask: When is the Day of Judgement?﴾: that is, when is the time of recompense? It is a question of denial and mockery. The reading of those who pronounced the hamza with a kasra in His saying ﴿When is its appointed time?﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 42] and ﴿When is the Day of Judgement?﴾ has already been mentioned, in which case the adverb is a locus for the verbal noun, and "their day" is governed by a hidden verb whose estimate is: it occurs, that is, the recompense, as said by al-Zajjāj. They also permitted that it be the predicate of a deleted subject, that is, it is their day, and the fatḥa is a fatḥa of indeclinability because it is annexed to a non-declinable word, and it is the nominal sentence. It is supported by the reading of Ibn Abī ʿAbla and al-Zaʿfarānī: "yawmuhum," with ḍamma. When it is an adverb, the vowel in it may be both a case-vowel and a built-vowel. The discussion of annexing the future adverb to a nominal sentence has already been treated in Ghāfir, in His saying: ﴿The day when they will emerge﴾ [Ghāfir: 16]. Some grammarians said: "yawmuhum" is a substitute for "yawm al-dīn," so here it is a narration of their speech in meaning, and they say that in the manner of mockery. Had it narrated the wording of their saying, the construction would have been: "the day when we shall be tormented over the Fire."

﴿Taste your trial﴾: that is, it will be said to them: taste. (This is): a subject and predicate. Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also permissible that "this" be a substitute for "your trial," that is, taste this punishment. End, and there is remoteness in it, and independence is better than substitution. The meaning of "you will be tried" is: you will be punished in the Fire.

When he mentioned the state of the disbelievers, he mentioned the state of the believers. ʿĀkhidhīn is in the accusative as a circumstantial, that is, receiving what He gives them, content with it, and that is in Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "ākhidhīn": that is, in their worldly life, ﴿what their Lord has given them﴾ of His commands, His prohibitions, and His law. So the circumstantial is narrated, since it precedes in time their being in Paradise. The apparent meaning is that "qalīlan" is an adverb, and it is originally an adjective, that is, they were in a little of the night. It was permitted that it be an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, that is, they used to sleep a little sleep, and "mā" is extra in both analyses. Anas ibn Mālik explained it, saying: they used to perform supererogatory prayers between maghrib and ʿishāʾ, and the wording of the verse does not indicate restriction to this explanation. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: they used to take a portion of the night. Muṭarrif, Mujāhid, and Ibn Abī Najīḥ said: the night that came upon them, almost all of it, was a sleepless one. Al-Ḥasan said: they struggled to stand in the night prayer, sleeping from it only a little. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: ﴿they were a little﴾, that is, in their number, and "thumma" is the predicate of "kānū," then he began: ﴿of the night they slept little﴾, so "mā" is a negation, and "qalīlan" is a good pause. This opinion involves dislocating the sentence, and the governed element of the negated operator preceded its operator with "mā," and that is not permitted according to the Basrans, even if it is an adverb or a prepositional phrase. Some have permitted it, and in poetry there is his saying:

When she stands up, bare-headed, her hair disheveled, the heart thinks her head is not veiled.

He placed "ra'sahā" before "mā tuqanna'u," and it is negated by "mā." They also permitted "mā" to be a verbal noun in the position of nominative with "qalīlan," that is, their sleep was little, and this is an easy and good construction, and that "mā" be a relative pronoun in the sense of "alladhī," with the returning pronoun deleted, its estimate: (p-136) ﴿they were a little of the night﴾ of the time in which they slept, and this involves strain. "Of the night" indicates that they were occupied with worship in times of rest and the calm of souls from the hardships of the day.

﴿And at dawn they ask forgiveness﴾: in this there is an indication that their tahajjud continued until dawn, so they began seeking forgiveness for what might have involved shortcoming, as if they had committed wrongs in those nights, and the dawns are the expected time of seeking forgiveness. Ibn ʿAmr al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "yastaghfirūn" means "yuṣallūn" (they pray). Al-Ḥasan said: they supplicate seeking forgiveness. The apparent meaning is that standing in the night and this right in wealth is among the recommended acts, and the greatest increase in reward comes from performing the recommended. Al-Qāḍī Mundhir ibn Saʿīd said: this right is the obligatory zakāh, and this was weakened on the ground that the sūrah is Meccan, and the obligation of zakāh was in Medina. It was said: it was obligatory and then abrogated, and this was weakened on the ground that God Most High did not legislate taking of wealth in Mecca before the Hijrah.

The sāʾil is the one who asks for charity, and the maḥrūm, linguistically, is the one prevented from something. ʿAlqamah said:

The one who feeds from the spoils on the day of spoils, his feeding is wherever he turns, and the deprived one remains deprived.

As for the verse, it is the one who is reckoned wealthy and so is deprived of charity because of his abstinence. It was also said: the one from whom the possibilities of provision are distant after being near, so that deprivation befalls him. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the maḥrūm is the one who has no share of wealth in Islam. Zayd ibn Aslam said: he is the one whose fruit has been destroyed by blight. It was said: the one whose livestock has died. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: he is the dog. It was said: the one whose wealth does not grow. It was said: the maḥrūf, the one who hardly ever earns. Other views were also said, and all these sayings are examples, not specifications, and what unites them is that he is the one who has no wealth due to a deprivation that befell him.

﴿And in the earth are signs﴾ that indicate the Maker, His power and His governance, in that it is like a carpet for what is above it, and in it are the mountain passes for travellers; and it is divided into plain and rugged, sea and land, and adjacent tracts of hard and soft, fertile and salt-marsh, and it is fertilized with kinds of plants; and in it are springs, minerals, and creatures scattered across its sea and land, differing in forms. Qatādah read: "āyatun," in the singular. (for those who have certainty): they are those who looked with sound reflection, and that led them to certainty in what the Messengers brought, so they became certain and no doubt entered them.

﴿And in yourselves﴾: at the beginning of their creation and their transition from state to state, and what He placed in the form of the human being of subtle senses, and what is arranged upon the intellect given to him of wondrous knowledge and strange crafts, and other things beyond counting.

﴿And in heaven is your provision﴾. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid, and Ibn Jubayr said: the rain and the snow, since it is the cause of sustenance, and every constant spring is from snow. Mujāhid also said, as did Wāṣil al-Aḥdab: he meant decree and destiny, that is, provision is with God, Who brings it as He wills. ﴿And what you are promised﴾: Paradise, or it is the Fire, or the matter of the Hour, or good and evil, or reward and punishment, sayings whose intent is example, not specification. Ibn Muḥaysin read: "arzāqukum," in the plural. The pronoun in "innahu" refers to the Qur'an, or to the religion in His saying ﴿and the religion is surely to come to pass﴾, or to the day mentioned in His saying ﴿When is the Day of Judgement?﴾, or to provision, or to God, or to the Prophet (ﷺ), these being reported sayings. What appears is that it refers to the preceding information from God Most High in this sūrah concerning the truth of the promise, the occurrence of recompense, their being in ﴿a discordant saying﴾, and ﴿Killed be the conjecturers﴾, and the abode of the God-fearing in Paradise as described, and the description of their qualities and what is mentioned after that. For this reason it is likened in reality to what is uttered by human speech, by the commonality they share in speech. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Bakr, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and al-Aʿmash, with variant transmissions from three of them, read "mithla" in the nominative as an attribute of "laḥaqq." The rest of the seven and the majority read it in the accusative. It was said: it is a fatḥa of indeclinability, and it is an attribute like its state in the reading of one who put it in the nominative. Since it was annexed to a non-declinable word it became indeclinable, and "mā" in this construction is extra for emphasis, and the annexation is to "annakum tanṭiqūn." Al-Māzinī said: "mithl" was built because it was compounded with "mā" and became one word, and similar to it are "waylamā" and "hayyamā" and "ibnamā." Ḥumayd ibn Thawr said:

Surely "hayyamā" for what I have met, and "hayyamā"; and woe to whoever has not met of them the "waylamā."

He said: were it not for the construction it would be nunated. Another poet said:

So honour us, a mother, and honour us, a son (ibnamā).

End of this derivation. "Ibnamā" is not a son built with "mā"; rather this is from the category of adding a mīm to it and following "mā" at the end, since the case-vowel was placed on the mīm. You say: "hādhā ibnam," "ra'aytu ibnamā," "marartu bi-ibnam," and the "mā" in the three cases in "ibnamā" is not compounded with "mā" as he said: the fatḥa in "ibnamā" is a case-vowel, and it is accusative as a specification. The grammarians cited the building of a noun with a particle in the verse of the rajaz:

Is it a bull that I hunt for you, or two bulls, or is it the hornless one with two horns?

It was said: it is an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, its estimate: "innahu la-ḥaqqun ḥaqqan mithla annakum," so its vowel is a case-vowel. It was said: it is accusative as a circumstantial of the pronoun concealed in "laḥaqq," and it was said: a circumstantial of "laḥaqq," though it is indefinite, and al-Jarmī and Sībawayh permitted that in various places of his book. Speech here is an expression for utterance with letters and sounds in the ordering of meanings. People say: "hādhā ḥaqq, as you are here," and "hādhā ḥaqq as you see and hear," and this is like the verse. "Mā" is extra according to the explicit statement of al-Khalīl, and its deletion is not transmitted, so you would not say: "hādhā ḥaqq ka-annaka hāhunā." The Kufans make "mithl" a locus and put it in the accusative as an adverb, and they permit "zaydun mithlaka" with the accusative, so according to their view "mithla" in it may be accusative as an adverb; their argument and the refutation of them is mentioned in grammar. Among the speech of some Bedouins: "Who is it that angered the Friend until he swore?" They did not believe him when he spoke, until they compelled him to the oath.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 51, verse 1–23 (part 1 of 2):

Surat adh-Dhariyat (The Scattering Winds), sixty verses, Meccan.
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)
﴿By the winds that scatter with dispersing,﴾ ﴿and those that bear the burden,﴾ ﴿and those that run with ease,﴾ ﴿and those that distribute by command,﴾ ﴿indeed what you are promised is surely true,﴾ ﴿and indeed the Recompense is surely to occur,﴾ ﴿by the sky with its paths,﴾ ﴿indeed you are in a contradictory saying,﴾ ﴿turned away from it is whoever is turned away,﴾ ﴿destroyed are the liars,﴾ ﴿who are in heedlessness, forgetful,﴾ ﴿they ask, "When is the Day of Recompense?"﴾ ﴿the Day they will be tried over the Fire,﴾ ﴿"Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten."﴾ ﴿Indeed the God-conscious will be in gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿taking what their Lord has given them; indeed they were before that good-doers,﴾ ﴿they used to sleep little of the night,﴾ ﴿and in the hours before dawn they would seek forgiveness,﴾ ﴿and in their wealth was a right for the beggar and the deprived,﴾ ﴿and in the earth are signs for those who are certain,﴾ ﴿and in yourselves; will you not then see?﴾ ﴿and in the sky is your provision and what you are promised,﴾ ﴿so by the Lord of the sky and the earth, indeed it is surely true, just as you speak.﴾ ﴿Has there reached you the story of Abraham's honored guests?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Peace, a people unknown."﴾ ﴿Then he went quickly to his family and brought a fat calf,﴾ ﴿and placed it before them, he said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿So he sensed fear of them; they said, "Do not fear," and gave him glad tidings of a knowing boy,﴾ ﴿Then his wife came forward crying out, and struck her face and said, "A barren old woman!"﴾ ﴿They said, "Thus said your Lord; indeed He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed we have been sent to a criminal people,﴾ ﴿to send upon them stones of clay,﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for the transgressors,﴾ ﴿so We brought out those of the believers who were there,﴾ ﴿but We found there not one house of Muslims,﴾ ﴿and We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment,﴾ ﴿and in Moses, when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority,﴾ ﴿but he turned away with his supporters and said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea, and he was blameworthy,﴾ ﴿and in 'Ad, when We sent upon them the barren wind,﴾ ﴿which left nothing it came upon without making it like crumbled dust,﴾ ﴿and in Thamud, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a while,"﴾ ﴿but they rebelled against the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on,﴾ ﴿and they were not able to stand up, nor were they among those who could defend themselves,﴾ ﴿and the people of Noah before, indeed they were a defiantly disobedient people,﴾ ﴿and the sky We built with power, and indeed We are expanding it,﴾ ﴿and the earth We spread out, and how excellent are the spreaders!﴾ ﴿And of every thing We created pairs, that perhaps you may remember,﴾ ﴿so flee to Allah; indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner,﴾ ﴿and do not set up with Allah another god; indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner.﴾ ﴿Thus no messenger came to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ ﴿Did they charge one another with it? No, they are a transgressing people.﴾ ﴿So turn away from them, and you are not to be blamed,﴾ ﴿and remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers.﴾ ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me,﴾ ﴿I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me.﴾ ﴿Indeed Allah is the Provider, Possessor of strength, the Firm.﴾ ﴿Indeed for those who did wrong is a portion like the portion of their companions, so let them not seek to hasten.﴾ ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved from their Day which they are promised.﴾)
(p-132) Al-hubuk: the paths, like the folds of sand and of still water when the wind strikes it, and likewise the hubuk of hair: the traces of its waviness and crinkling. The poet said:
A poem: "Covered with the roots of the star, woven by a cold wind over the bright surface of its water, hubuk."
The coat of mail is called mahbuka because its rings are fashioned into paths. Its singular is habika, like tariqa and turuq, or hibak like mithal and mithl. The rajaz poet said:
A poem: "As if the weaver had woven it, a carpet with its weft-work hibak."
It is said: hibak is the cord with which the cane-cutter ties his bundle, a long strip made in the arrangement of the rows of planted trees. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "I made the thing firm and did its work well." Al-Farra' said: al-hubuk is the crumpling of everything. Others said: al-mahbuk is the strongly formed one, of a horse or otherwise. Imru' al-Qays said:
A poem: "He has come bearing me on his nose, a swift-stepping, strongly built, firmly made one."
Al-huju': sleep. As-simn: well known, the filling of the body with fat and flesh. It is said: samina, simanan, fa-huwa samin; they departed from the norm in the verbal noun and the active participle, and the analogy would be samina and sammana. They also said: samin, when he has become fat. Adh-dhanub: the great bucket. The rajaz poet said:
A poem: "Indeed, when a stranger attacks us, he has a bucket and we have a bucket, and if you refuse, then we have the well."
Az-Zamakhshari recited it: "For us a bucket, and for you a bucket." It is also used to mean share and portion. 'Alqama ibn 'Abda said:
A poem: "And in every tribe you have spread blessing, so a portion is due to Shas from your generosity."
Az-Zamakhshari attributed it to 'Amr ibn Shas, which is an error in the Diwan of 'Alqama. Al-Harith ibn Abi Shimr al-Ghassani had captured Shas, brother of 'Alqama, so 'Alqama entered to him and praised him with the qasida in which this verse is. When he reached this verse in the recitation, al-Harith said: "Yes, and he has given it." Hassan said:
A poem: "Let Rabi'a ibn Mukarram not be far, and may the morning clouds water his grave with buckets."
Another said:
A poem: "By your life, and the fates are coming, for every son of a father there is a bucket of them."
(p-133) [Quranic text repeated as above]
This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what came before it is that He said: "So remind with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning." At the beginning of this one, after the oath, He said: "Indeed what you are promised is surely true, and indeed the Recompense is surely to occur."
﴿Adh-dhariyat﴾: the winds.
﴿Al-hamilat﴾: the clouds.
﴿Al-jariyat﴾: the ships.
﴿Al-muqassimat﴾: the angels. This is the explanation of 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, from the pulpit, when Ibn al-Kawwa' asked him; it was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas also said: ﴿al-hamilat﴾ are the ships laden with people and their goods. It was said: the carriers are all animals. It was said: al-jariyat are the clouds moved by the winds. It was said: al-jawari are the stars. Abu 'Amr and Hamza assimilated the dhal of ﴿adh-dhariyat﴾ into the dhal of (dharwan), and its scattering is dispersing it for rain or for dust. It was read with a fatha on the waw, naming what is carried by the verbal noun. The meaning of (yusran) is a course with ease, that is, facility. So yusran is a verbal noun described by it with an omitted supposition, so it is in the position of a circumstantial accusative according to Sibawayh's view. (Amran): they distribute affairs of rains, provisions and other things, so amran is the object. It was said: it is a verbal noun in the accusative of circumstance, meaning commanded, and the object of al-muqassimat is omitted. Mujahid said: the affair of the servants is handled by Jibril for harshness, Mika'il for mercy, the Angel of Death for seizing souls, and Israfil for the blowing. About the angels it came: al-muqassimat in the sense of groups. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that the winds alone are meant, because they produce the clouds, carry them, direct them, and move through the air with easy motion, and distribute the rain by the turning of the winds. End of quote. If the referents differ, these are successive divisions. If they do not differ, it is one division, and it is from the conjunction of attributes: they scatter dust and pebbles at the start of their blowing, then they carry the clouds, then run through the air spreading the clouds, then distribute the rain. This is like his saying:
A poem: "Alas for Zayyaba for al-Harith, the one who attacks at dawn, the one who takes booty, the one who returns."
That is: the one who attacked the enemy at dawn, took booty from them, and returned to his people safe and victorious. The sentence sworn to, which is the answer of the oath, is ﴿Indeed what you are promised﴾, and ma is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," with the returning pronoun omitted, that is, you are promised it. It is possible that it is a verbal noun, that is, its promise to you or its threat, since "you are promised" can carry both meanings, being the present of "wa'ada" and the present of "awda'a." It fits being the present of "awda'a" because of His saying: ﴿So remind with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾, and because the intent is intimidation and awe. The meaning of its truth is the certainty of its occurrence, and the one who is truly described as truthful is the one who informs. He said: ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾: that is, one in which truth is found. It was said: (lasadiq), and he placed the active participle in the position of the verbal noun, and there is no need for this supposition. Mujahid said: the more apparent view is that the verse concerns the disbelievers, and that it is pure threat.
﴿And indeed the Recompense﴾: that is, the reward, (lawaqi'): that is, truly issuing upon the responsible ones from mankind and jinn. The apparent meaning of "in the sky" is that it is a collective noun, by which all the heavens are meant. Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As said: it is the seventh heaven. It was said: the cloud that shades the earth.
﴿Dhat al-hubuk﴾: that is, possessing a level, good creation. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Qatada and al-Rabi'. Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿dhat al-hubuk﴾: that is, adorned with stars. Ad-Dahhak said: possessing paths, meaning the Milky Way in the sky. Ibn Zayd said: possessing strength, due to His saying: ﴿seven strong ones﴾ [al-Naba' 12]. It was said: possessing firmness.
The majority read al-hubuk with two dammas. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, with a variant from him, Abu Malik al-Ghifari, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu al-Sammal and Nu'aym from Abu 'Amr read it with a sukun on the ba'. 'Ikrima read it with a fatha, as the plural of habaka, like tarfa and turaf. Abu Malik al-Ghifari and al-Hasan, with a variant from him, read it with a kasra on the ha and ba'. Abu Malik al-Ghifari, al-Hasan also, and Abu Haywa read it with a kasra on the ha and a sukun on the ba', and this is the lightening of fi'il with both kasras, and it is a singular noun, not a plural, because fi'il is not among the patterns of plurals, so it should be counted with ibil among what came as nouns of the pattern fi'il with kasra on the fa and ayn. Ibn 'Abbas also and Abu Malik read it with fatha on both. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: it is the plural of habaka, like 'aqaba and 'aqab. End of quote. Al-Hasan also: al-hibak, with a kasra on the ha and a fatha on the ba'. He also read as the majority did, so his reading became five: al-hubuk, al-hibuk, al-hubk, al-hubak, al-habak. Abu Malik also read: al-hibuk with a kasra on the ha and a damma on the ba', and Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned it from al-Hasan, so he has six readings. The author of al-Lawami', who is unmatched in Arabic in its patterns and measures, said: "I do not know what transmitted it." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is an anomalous reading, not well founded, and it seems he meant the kasra, then imagined "al-hibuk" as the reading with damma after reading the ha with kasra and the ba' with damma, and this is by intermixing of dialects, and this pattern is not found in Arab speech. End of quote.

Thus the grammarians interpreted these readings, but in my view the better reading is that it belongs to those cases where the vowel of the ḥāʾ follows the vowel of dhāt in the kasra, and the unvowelled lām is not taken into account, because a quiescent letter is a weak barrier. The response to the oath is: ﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾. The apparent meaning is that it is a general address to both the believer and the disbeliever, just as the response to the earlier oath includes both of them, and their discord is that some of them are believers in the Messenger (ﷺ) and his Book, and some are disbelievers. Ibn Zayd said: it is an address to the disbelievers, who say: "a sorcerer, a poet, a soothsayer, a madman." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the speech of the disbelievers cannot be consistent; rather it is contradictory and discordant. It was also said: their discord concerns the Resurrection, some of them denying it and some doubting it. It was also said: their discord is their acknowledgement that God Most High brought them into existence, while they worship other than Him, and the sayings they utter about their gods.

(yu'faku): that is, he is turned away from it, that is, from the Qur'an and the Messenger (ﷺ), as said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah.

﴿Whoever is turned away﴾: that is, whoever is turned away with the turning that admits of no greater or more severe turning, in keeping with his saying: "None perishes before God except one who is destined to perish." It was also said: whoever is turned away in the foreknowledge of God Most High, meaning that he is one who is turned away from the truth and does not desist. Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to what you are promised, or to the one who swore by the heaven (p-135) that they are in a discordant saying regarding its occurrence, so some of them are doubtful and some of them are deniers. Then he said: "is turned away from belief in the matter of the Resurrection is the one who is turned away." It was also said: the one turned away from is omitted, and ʿan here denotes cause, and the pronoun refers to ﴿a discordant saying﴾, meaning that by means of it is turned away whoever wishes to embrace Islam, by saying: "It is sorcery; it is soothsaying." This was related by al-Zahrāwī and al-Zamakhsharī, and he presented it, in his customary manner of presenting what is reported from others as his own invention. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: It is possible that it refers to ﴿a discordant saying﴾, and the meaning is: whoever has his happiness prevail is turned away from it by God's granting of success into Islam; and this is on the basis that it is a discordant saying of the disbelievers, except that the usage of the idiom in its falsehood is turning from good to evil, and therefore you find it only in those who are blamed. End, and there is some abridgement in it. Ibn Jubayr and Qatādah read: "man afaka," with the active voice, meaning: whoever the people have turned away from it, and they are the Quraysh. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read: "ya'fiku ʿanhu man afaka," meaning: whoever is himself turned away turns people away from it. Also from him: "ya'fiku ʿanhu man afaka," meaning: whoever is a great liar turns people away from it. And it was read: "yu'fanu ʿanhu man afana," with nūn in both, meaning: whoever is deprived is deprived of it, from afana al-ḍarʿ, when he milked it to exhaustion.

﴿Killed be the conjecturers﴾: that is, God has destroyed the conjecturers, who are those who estimate what is not valid.

﴿In a heedless state﴾: in ignorance that overwhelms them. (heedless): unmindful of what they were commanded.

﴿They ask: When is the Day of Judgement?﴾: that is, when is the time of recompense? It is a question of denial and mockery. The reading of those who pronounced the hamza with a kasra in His saying ﴿When is its appointed time?﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 42] and ﴿When is the Day of Judgement?﴾ has already been mentioned, in which case the adverb is a locus for the verbal noun, and "their day" is governed by a hidden verb whose estimate is: it occurs, that is, the recompense, as said by al-Zajjāj. They also permitted that it be the predicate of a deleted subject, that is, it is their day, and the fatḥa is a fatḥa of indeclinability because it is annexed to a non-declinable word, and it is the nominal sentence. It is supported by the reading of Ibn Abī ʿAbla and al-Zaʿfarānī: "yawmuhum," with ḍamma. When it is an adverb, the vowel in it may be both a case-vowel and a built-vowel. The discussion of annexing the future adverb to a nominal sentence has already been treated in Ghāfir, in His saying: ﴿The day when they will emerge﴾ [Ghāfir: 16]. Some grammarians said: "yawmuhum" is a substitute for "yawm al-dīn," so here it is a narration of their speech in meaning, and they say that in the manner of mockery. Had it narrated the wording of their saying, the construction would have been: "the day when we shall be tormented over the Fire."

﴿Taste your trial﴾: that is, it will be said to them: taste. (This is): a subject and predicate. Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also permissible that "this" be a substitute for "your trial," that is, taste this punishment. End, and there is remoteness in it, and independence is better than substitution. The meaning of "you will be tried" is: you will be punished in the Fire.

When he mentioned the state of the disbelievers, he mentioned the state of the believers. ʿĀkhidhīn is in the accusative as a circumstantial, that is, receiving what He gives them, content with it, and that is in Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "ākhidhīn": that is, in their worldly life, ﴿what their Lord has given them﴾ of His commands, His prohibitions, and His law. So the circumstantial is narrated, since it precedes in time their being in Paradise. The apparent meaning is that "qalīlan" is an adverb, and it is originally an adjective, that is, they were in a little of the night. It was permitted that it be an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, that is, they used to sleep a little sleep, and "mā" is extra in both analyses. Anas ibn Mālik explained it, saying: they used to perform supererogatory prayers between maghrib and ʿishāʾ, and the wording of the verse does not indicate restriction to this explanation. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: they used to take a portion of the night. Muṭarrif, Mujāhid, and Ibn Abī Najīḥ said: the night that came upon them, almost all of it, was a sleepless one. Al-Ḥasan said: they struggled to stand in the night prayer, sleeping from it only a little. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: ﴿they were a little﴾, that is, in their number, and "thumma" is the predicate of "kānū," then he began: ﴿of the night they slept little﴾, so "mā" is a negation, and "qalīlan" is a good pause. This opinion involves dislocating the sentence, and the governed element of the negated operator preceded its operator with "mā," and that is not permitted according to the Basrans, even if it is an adverb or a prepositional phrase. Some have permitted it, and in poetry there is his saying:

When she stands up, bare-headed, her hair disheveled, the heart thinks her head is not veiled.

He placed "ra'sahā" before "mā tuqanna'u," and it is negated by "mā." They also permitted "mā" to be a verbal noun in the position of nominative with "qalīlan," that is, their sleep was little, and this is an easy and good construction, and that "mā" be a relative pronoun in the sense of "alladhī," with the returning pronoun deleted, its estimate: (p-136) ﴿they were a little of the night﴾ of the time in which they slept, and this involves strain. "Of the night" indicates that they were occupied with worship in times of rest and the calm of souls from the hardships of the day.

﴿And at dawn they ask forgiveness﴾: in this there is an indication that their tahajjud continued until dawn, so they began seeking forgiveness for what might have involved shortcoming, as if they had committed wrongs in those nights, and the dawns are the expected time of seeking forgiveness. Ibn ʿAmr al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "yastaghfirūn" means "yuṣallūn" (they pray). Al-Ḥasan said: they supplicate seeking forgiveness. The apparent meaning is that standing in the night and this right in wealth is among the recommended acts, and the greatest increase in reward comes from performing the recommended. Al-Qāḍī Mundhir ibn Saʿīd said: this right is the obligatory zakāh, and this was weakened on the ground that the sūrah is Meccan, and the obligation of zakāh was in Medina. It was said: it was obligatory and then abrogated, and this was weakened on the ground that God Most High did not legislate taking of wealth in Mecca before the Hijrah.

The sāʾil is the one who asks for charity, and the maḥrūm, linguistically, is the one prevented from something. ʿAlqamah said:

The one who feeds from the spoils on the day of spoils, his feeding is wherever he turns, and the deprived one remains deprived.

As for the verse, it is the one who is reckoned wealthy and so is deprived of charity because of his abstinence. It was also said: the one from whom the possibilities of provision are distant after being near, so that deprivation befalls him. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the maḥrūm is the one who has no share of wealth in Islam. Zayd ibn Aslam said: he is the one whose fruit has been destroyed by blight. It was said: the one whose livestock has died. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: he is the dog. It was said: the one whose wealth does not grow. It was said: the maḥrūf, the one who hardly ever earns. Other views were also said, and all these sayings are examples, not specifications, and what unites them is that he is the one who has no wealth due to a deprivation that befell him.

﴿And in the earth are signs﴾ that indicate the Maker, His power and His governance, in that it is like a carpet for what is above it, and in it are the mountain passes for travellers; and it is divided into plain and rugged, sea and land, and adjacent tracts of hard and soft, fertile and salt-marsh, and it is fertilized with kinds of plants; and in it are springs, minerals, and creatures scattered across its sea and land, differing in forms. Qatādah read: "āyatun," in the singular. (for those who have certainty): they are those who looked with sound reflection, and that led them to certainty in what the Messengers brought, so they became certain and no doubt entered them.

﴿And in yourselves﴾: at the beginning of their creation and their transition from state to state, and what He placed in the form of the human being of subtle senses, and what is arranged upon the intellect given to him of wondrous knowledge and strange crafts, and other things beyond counting.

﴿And in heaven is your provision﴾. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid, and Ibn Jubayr said: the rain and the snow, since it is the cause of sustenance, and every constant spring is from snow. Mujāhid also said, as did Wāṣil al-Aḥdab: he meant decree and destiny, that is, provision is with God, Who brings it as He wills. ﴿And what you are promised﴾: Paradise, or it is the Fire, or the matter of the Hour, or good and evil, or reward and punishment, sayings whose intent is example, not specification. Ibn Muḥaysin read: "arzāqukum," in the plural. The pronoun in "innahu" refers to the Qur'an, or to the religion in His saying ﴿and the religion is surely to come to pass﴾, or to the day mentioned in His saying ﴿When is the Day of Judgement?﴾, or to provision, or to God, or to the Prophet (ﷺ), these being reported sayings. What appears is that it refers to the preceding information from God Most High in this sūrah concerning the truth of the promise, the occurrence of recompense, their being in ﴿a discordant saying﴾, and ﴿Killed be the conjecturers﴾, and the abode of the God-fearing in Paradise as described, and the description of their qualities and what is mentioned after that. For this reason it is likened in reality to what is uttered by human speech, by the commonality they share in speech. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Bakr, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and al-Aʿmash, with variant transmissions from three of them, read "mithla" in the nominative as an attribute of "laḥaqq." The rest of the seven and the majority read it in the accusative. It was said: it is a fatḥa of indeclinability, and it is an attribute like its state in the reading of one who put it in the nominative. Since it was annexed to a non-declinable word it became indeclinable, and "mā" in this construction is extra for emphasis, and the annexation is to "annakum tanṭiqūn." Al-Māzinī said: "mithl" was built because it was compounded with "mā" and became one word, and similar to it are "waylamā" and "hayyamā" and "ibnamā." Ḥumayd ibn Thawr said:

Surely "hayyamā" for what I have met, and "hayyamā"; and woe to whoever has not met of them the "waylamā."

He said: were it not for the construction it would be nunated. Another poet said:

So honour us, a mother, and honour us, a son (ibnamā).

End of this derivation. "Ibnamā" is not a son built with "mā"; rather this is from the category of adding a mīm to it and following "mā" at the end, since the case-vowel was placed on the mīm. You say: "hādhā ibnam," "ra'aytu ibnamā," "marartu bi-ibnam," and the "mā" in the three cases in "ibnamā" is not compounded with "mā" as he said: the fatḥa in "ibnamā" is a case-vowel, and it is accusative as a specification. The grammarians cited the building of a noun with a particle in the verse of the rajaz:

Is it a bull that I hunt for you, or two bulls, or is it the hornless one with two horns?

It was said: it is an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, its estimate: "innahu la-ḥaqqun ḥaqqan mithla annakum," so its vowel is a case-vowel. It was said: it is accusative as a circumstantial of the pronoun concealed in "laḥaqq," and it was said: a circumstantial of "laḥaqq," though it is indefinite, and al-Jarmī and Sībawayh permitted that in various places of his book. Speech here is an expression for utterance with letters and sounds in the ordering of meanings. People say: "hādhā ḥaqq, as you are here," and "hādhā ḥaqq as you see and hear," and this is like the verse. "Mā" is extra according to the explicit statement of al-Khalīl, and its deletion is not transmitted, so you would not say: "hādhā ḥaqq ka-annaka hāhunā." The Kufans make "mithl" a locus and put it in the accusative as an adverb, and they permit "zaydun mithlaka" with the accusative, so according to their view "mithla" in it may be accusative as an adverb; their argument and the refutation of them is mentioned in grammar. Among the speech of some Bedouins: "Who is it that angered the Friend until he swore?" They did not believe him when he spoke, until they compelled him to the oath.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 51, verse 1–23 (part 1 of 2):

Surat adh-Dhariyat (The Scattering Winds), sixty verses, Meccan.
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)
﴿By the winds that scatter with dispersing,﴾ ﴿and those that bear the burden,﴾ ﴿and those that run with ease,﴾ ﴿and those that distribute by command,﴾ ﴿indeed what you are promised is surely true,﴾ ﴿and indeed the Recompense is surely to occur,﴾ ﴿by the sky with its paths,﴾ ﴿indeed you are in a contradictory saying,﴾ ﴿turned away from it is whoever is turned away,﴾ ﴿destroyed are the liars,﴾ ﴿who are in heedlessness, forgetful,﴾ ﴿they ask, "When is the Day of Recompense?"﴾ ﴿the Day they will be tried over the Fire,﴾ ﴿"Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten."﴾ ﴿Indeed the God-conscious will be in gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿taking what their Lord has given them; indeed they were before that good-doers,﴾ ﴿they used to sleep little of the night,﴾ ﴿and in the hours before dawn they would seek forgiveness,﴾ ﴿and in their wealth was a right for the beggar and the deprived,﴾ ﴿and in the earth are signs for those who are certain,﴾ ﴿and in yourselves; will you not then see?﴾ ﴿and in the sky is your provision and what you are promised,﴾ ﴿so by the Lord of the sky and the earth, indeed it is surely true, just as you speak.﴾ ﴿Has there reached you the story of Abraham's honored guests?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Peace, a people unknown."﴾ ﴿Then he went quickly to his family and brought a fat calf,﴾ ﴿and placed it before them, he said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿So he sensed fear of them; they said, "Do not fear," and gave him glad tidings of a knowing boy,﴾ ﴿Then his wife came forward crying out, and struck her face and said, "A barren old woman!"﴾ ﴿They said, "Thus said your Lord; indeed He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed we have been sent to a criminal people,﴾ ﴿to send upon them stones of clay,﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for the transgressors,﴾ ﴿so We brought out those of the believers who were there,﴾ ﴿but We found there not one house of Muslims,﴾ ﴿and We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment,﴾ ﴿and in Moses, when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority,﴾ ﴿but he turned away with his supporters and said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea, and he was blameworthy,﴾ ﴿and in 'Ad, when We sent upon them the barren wind,﴾ ﴿which left nothing it came upon without making it like crumbled dust,﴾ ﴿and in Thamud, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a while,"﴾ ﴿but they rebelled against the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on,﴾ ﴿and they were not able to stand up, nor were they among those who could defend themselves,﴾ ﴿and the people of Noah before, indeed they were a defiantly disobedient people,﴾ ﴿and the sky We built with power, and indeed We are expanding it,﴾ ﴿and the earth We spread out, and how excellent are the spreaders!﴾ ﴿And of every thing We created pairs, that perhaps you may remember,﴾ ﴿so flee to Allah; indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner,﴾ ﴿and do not set up with Allah another god; indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner.﴾ ﴿Thus no messenger came to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ ﴿Did they charge one another with it? No, they are a transgressing people.﴾ ﴿So turn away from them, and you are not to be blamed,﴾ ﴿and remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers.﴾ ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me,﴾ ﴿I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me.﴾ ﴿Indeed Allah is the Provider, Possessor of strength, the Firm.﴾ ﴿Indeed for those who did wrong is a portion like the portion of their companions, so let them not seek to hasten.﴾ ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved from their Day which they are promised.﴾)
(p-132) Al-hubuk: the paths, like the folds of sand and of still water when the wind strikes it, and likewise the hubuk of hair: the traces of its waviness and crinkling. The poet said:
A poem: "Covered with the roots of the star, woven by a cold wind over the bright surface of its water, hubuk."
The coat of mail is called mahbuka because its rings are fashioned into paths. Its singular is habika, like tariqa and turuq, or hibak like mithal and mithl. The rajaz poet said:
A poem: "As if the weaver had woven it, a carpet with its weft-work hibak."
It is said: hibak is the cord with which the cane-cutter ties his bundle, a long strip made in the arrangement of the rows of planted trees. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "I made the thing firm and did its work well." Al-Farra' said: al-hubuk is the crumpling of everything. Others said: al-mahbuk is the strongly formed one, of a horse or otherwise. Imru' al-Qays said:
A poem: "He has come bearing me on his nose, a swift-stepping, strongly built, firmly made one."
Al-huju': sleep. As-simn: well known, the filling of the body with fat and flesh. It is said: samina, simanan, fa-huwa samin; they departed from the norm in the verbal noun and the active participle, and the analogy would be samina and sammana. They also said: samin, when he has become fat. Adh-dhanub: the great bucket. The rajaz poet said:
A poem: "Indeed, when a stranger attacks us, he has a bucket and we have a bucket, and if you refuse, then we have the well."
Az-Zamakhshari recited it: "For us a bucket, and for you a bucket." It is also used to mean share and portion. 'Alqama ibn 'Abda said:
A poem: "And in every tribe you have spread blessing, so a portion is due to Shas from your generosity."
Az-Zamakhshari attributed it to 'Amr ibn Shas, which is an error in the Diwan of 'Alqama. Al-Harith ibn Abi Shimr al-Ghassani had captured Shas, brother of 'Alqama, so 'Alqama entered to him and praised him with the qasida in which this verse is. When he reached this verse in the recitation, al-Harith said: "Yes, and he has given it." Hassan said:
A poem: "Let Rabi'a ibn Mukarram not be far, and may the morning clouds water his grave with buckets."
Another said:
A poem: "By your life, and the fates are coming, for every son of a father there is a bucket of them."
(p-133) [Quranic text repeated as above]
This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what came before it is that He said: "So remind with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning." At the beginning of this one, after the oath, He said: "Indeed what you are promised is surely true, and indeed the Recompense is surely to occur."
﴿Adh-dhariyat﴾: the winds.
﴿Al-hamilat﴾: the clouds.
﴿Al-jariyat﴾: the ships.
﴿Al-muqassimat﴾: the angels. This is the explanation of 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, from the pulpit, when Ibn al-Kawwa' asked him; it was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas also said: ﴿al-hamilat﴾ are the ships laden with people and their goods. It was said: the carriers are all animals. It was said: al-jariyat are the clouds moved by the winds. It was said: al-jawari are the stars. Abu 'Amr and Hamza assimilated the dhal of ﴿adh-dhariyat﴾ into the dhal of (dharwan), and its scattering is dispersing it for rain or for dust. It was read with a fatha on the waw, naming what is carried by the verbal noun. The meaning of (yusran) is a course with ease, that is, facility. So yusran is a verbal noun described by it with an omitted supposition, so it is in the position of a circumstantial accusative according to Sibawayh's view. (Amran): they distribute affairs of rains, provisions and other things, so amran is the object. It was said: it is a verbal noun in the accusative of circumstance, meaning commanded, and the object of al-muqassimat is omitted. Mujahid said: the affair of the servants is handled by Jibril for harshness, Mika'il for mercy, the Angel of Death for seizing souls, and Israfil for the blowing. About the angels it came: al-muqassimat in the sense of groups. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that the winds alone are meant, because they produce the clouds, carry them, direct them, and move through the air with easy motion, and distribute the rain by the turning of the winds. End of quote. If the referents differ, these are successive divisions. If they do not differ, it is one division, and it is from the conjunction of attributes: they scatter dust and pebbles at the start of their blowing, then they carry the clouds, then run through the air spreading the clouds, then distribute the rain. This is like his saying:
A poem: "Alas for Zayyaba for al-Harith, the one who attacks at dawn, the one who takes booty, the one who returns."
That is: the one who attacked the enemy at dawn, took booty from them, and returned to his people safe and victorious. The sentence sworn to, which is the answer of the oath, is ﴿Indeed what you are promised﴾, and ma is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," with the returning pronoun omitted, that is, you are promised it. It is possible that it is a verbal noun, that is, its promise to you or its threat, since "you are promised" can carry both meanings, being the present of "wa'ada" and the present of "awda'a." It fits being the present of "awda'a" because of His saying: ﴿So remind with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾, and because the intent is intimidation and awe. The meaning of its truth is the certainty of its occurrence, and the one who is truly described as truthful is the one who informs. He said: ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾: that is, one in which truth is found. It was said: (lasadiq), and he placed the active participle in the position of the verbal noun, and there is no need for this supposition. Mujahid said: the more apparent view is that the verse concerns the disbelievers, and that it is pure threat.
﴿And indeed the Recompense﴾: that is, the reward, (lawaqi'): that is, truly issuing upon the responsible ones from mankind and jinn. The apparent meaning of "in the sky" is that it is a collective noun, by which all the heavens are meant. Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As said: it is the seventh heaven. It was said: the cloud that shades the earth.
﴿Dhat al-hubuk﴾: that is, possessing a level, good creation. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Qatada and al-Rabi'. Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿dhat al-hubuk﴾: that is, adorned with stars. Ad-Dahhak said: possessing paths, meaning the Milky Way in the sky. Ibn Zayd said: possessing strength, due to His saying: ﴿seven strong ones﴾ [al-Naba' 12]. It was said: possessing firmness.
The majority read al-hubuk with two dammas. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, with a variant from him, Abu Malik al-Ghifari, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu al-Sammal and Nu'aym from Abu 'Amr read it with a sukun on the ba'. 'Ikrima read it with a fatha, as the plural of habaka, like tarfa and turaf. Abu Malik al-Ghifari and al-Hasan, with a variant from him, read it with a kasra on the ha and ba'. Abu Malik al-Ghifari, al-Hasan also, and Abu Haywa read it with a kasra on the ha and a sukun on the ba', and this is the lightening of fi'il with both kasras, and it is a singular noun, not a plural, because fi'il is not among the patterns of plurals, so it should be counted with ibil among what came as nouns of the pattern fi'il with kasra on the fa and ayn. Ibn 'Abbas also and Abu Malik read it with fatha on both. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: it is the plural of habaka, like 'aqaba and 'aqab. End of quote. Al-Hasan also: al-hibak, with a kasra on the ha and a fatha on the ba'. He also read as the majority did, so his reading became five: al-hubuk, al-hibuk, al-hubk, al-hubak, al-habak. Abu Malik also read: al-hibuk with a kasra on the ha and a damma on the ba', and Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned it from al-Hasan, so he has six readings. The author of al-Lawami', who is unmatched in Arabic in its patterns and measures, said: "I do not know what transmitted it." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is an anomalous reading, not well founded, and it seems he meant the kasra, then imagined "al-hibuk" as the reading with damma after reading the ha with kasra and the ba' with damma, and this is by intermixing of dialects, and this pattern is not found in Arab speech. End of quote.

Thus the grammarians interpreted these readings, but in my view the better reading is that it belongs to those cases where the vowel of the ḥāʾ follows the vowel of dhāt in the kasra, and the unvowelled lām is not taken into account, because a quiescent letter is a weak barrier. The response to the oath is: ﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾. The apparent meaning is that it is a general address to both the believer and the disbeliever, just as the response to the earlier oath includes both of them, and their discord is that some of them are believers in the Messenger (ﷺ) and his Book, and some are disbelievers. Ibn Zayd said: it is an address to the disbelievers, who say: "a sorcerer, a poet, a soothsayer, a madman." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the speech of the disbelievers cannot be consistent; rather it is contradictory and discordant. It was also said: their discord concerns the Resurrection, some of them denying it and some doubting it. It was also said: their discord is their acknowledgement that God Most High brought them into existence, while they worship other than Him, and the sayings they utter about their gods.

(yu'faku): that is, he is turned away from it, that is, from the Qur'an and the Messenger (ﷺ), as said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah.

﴿Whoever is turned away﴾: that is, whoever is turned away with the turning that admits of no greater or more severe turning, in keeping with his saying: "None perishes before God except one who is destined to perish." It was also said: whoever is turned away in the foreknowledge of God Most High, meaning that he is one who is turned away from the truth and does not desist. Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to what you are promised, or to the one who swore by the heaven (p-135) that they are in a discordant saying regarding its occurrence, so some of them are doubtful and some of them are deniers. Then he said: "is turned away from belief in the matter of the Resurrection is the one who is turned away." It was also said: the one turned away from is omitted, and ʿan here denotes cause, and the pronoun refers to ﴿a discordant saying﴾, meaning that by means of it is turned away whoever wishes to embrace Islam, by saying: "It is sorcery; it is soothsaying." This was related by al-Zahrāwī and al-Zamakhsharī, and he presented it, in his customary manner of presenting what is reported from others as his own invention. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: It is possible that it refers to ﴿a discordant saying﴾, and the meaning is: whoever has his happiness prevail is turned away from it by God's granting of success into Islam; and this is on the basis that it is a discordant saying of the disbelievers, except that the usage of the idiom in its falsehood is turning from good to evil, and therefore you find it only in those who are blamed. End, and there is some abridgement in it. Ibn Jubayr and Qatādah read: "man afaka," with the active voice, meaning: whoever the people have turned away from it, and they are the Quraysh. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read: "ya'fiku ʿanhu man afaka," meaning: whoever is himself turned away turns people away from it. Also from him: "ya'fiku ʿanhu man afaka," meaning: whoever is a great liar turns people away from it. And it was read: "yu'fanu ʿanhu man afana," with nūn in both, meaning: whoever is deprived is deprived of it, from afana al-ḍarʿ, when he milked it to exhaustion.

﴿Killed be the conjecturers﴾: that is, God has destroyed the conjecturers, who are those who estimate what is not valid.

﴿In a heedless state﴾: in ignorance that overwhelms them. (heedless): unmindful of what they were commanded.

﴿They ask: When is the Day of Judgement?﴾: that is, when is the time of recompense? It is a question of denial and mockery. The reading of those who pronounced the hamza with a kasra in His saying ﴿When is its appointed time?﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 42] and ﴿When is the Day of Judgement?﴾ has already been mentioned, in which case the adverb is a locus for the verbal noun, and "their day" is governed by a hidden verb whose estimate is: it occurs, that is, the recompense, as said by al-Zajjāj. They also permitted that it be the predicate of a deleted subject, that is, it is their day, and the fatḥa is a fatḥa of indeclinability because it is annexed to a non-declinable word, and it is the nominal sentence. It is supported by the reading of Ibn Abī ʿAbla and al-Zaʿfarānī: "yawmuhum," with ḍamma. When it is an adverb, the vowel in it may be both a case-vowel and a built-vowel. The discussion of annexing the future adverb to a nominal sentence has already been treated in Ghāfir, in His saying: ﴿The day when they will emerge﴾ [Ghāfir: 16]. Some grammarians said: "yawmuhum" is a substitute for "yawm al-dīn," so here it is a narration of their speech in meaning, and they say that in the manner of mockery. Had it narrated the wording of their saying, the construction would have been: "the day when we shall be tormented over the Fire."

﴿Taste your trial﴾: that is, it will be said to them: taste. (This is): a subject and predicate. Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also permissible that "this" be a substitute for "your trial," that is, taste this punishment. End, and there is remoteness in it, and independence is better than substitution. The meaning of "you will be tried" is: you will be punished in the Fire.

When he mentioned the state of the disbelievers, he mentioned the state of the believers. ʿĀkhidhīn is in the accusative as a circumstantial, that is, receiving what He gives them, content with it, and that is in Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "ākhidhīn": that is, in their worldly life, ﴿what their Lord has given them﴾ of His commands, His prohibitions, and His law. So the circumstantial is narrated, since it precedes in time their being in Paradise. The apparent meaning is that "qalīlan" is an adverb, and it is originally an adjective, that is, they were in a little of the night. It was permitted that it be an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, that is, they used to sleep a little sleep, and "mā" is extra in both analyses. Anas ibn Mālik explained it, saying: they used to perform supererogatory prayers between maghrib and ʿishāʾ, and the wording of the verse does not indicate restriction to this explanation. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: they used to take a portion of the night. Muṭarrif, Mujāhid, and Ibn Abī Najīḥ said: the night that came upon them, almost all of it, was a sleepless one. Al-Ḥasan said: they struggled to stand in the night prayer, sleeping from it only a little. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: ﴿they were a little﴾, that is, in their number, and "thumma" is the predicate of "kānū," then he began: ﴿of the night they slept little﴾, so "mā" is a negation, and "qalīlan" is a good pause. This opinion involves dislocating the sentence, and the governed element of the negated operator preceded its operator with "mā," and that is not permitted according to the Basrans, even if it is an adverb or a prepositional phrase. Some have permitted it, and in poetry there is his saying:

When she stands up, bare-headed, her hair disheveled, the heart thinks her head is not veiled.

He placed "ra'sahā" before "mā tuqanna'u," and it is negated by "mā." They also permitted "mā" to be a verbal noun in the position of nominative with "qalīlan," that is, their sleep was little, and this is an easy and good construction, and that "mā" be a relative pronoun in the sense of "alladhī," with the returning pronoun deleted, its estimate: (p-136) ﴿they were a little of the night﴾ of the time in which they slept, and this involves strain. "Of the night" indicates that they were occupied with worship in times of rest and the calm of souls from the hardships of the day.

﴿And at dawn they ask forgiveness﴾: in this there is an indication that their tahajjud continued until dawn, so they began seeking forgiveness for what might have involved shortcoming, as if they had committed wrongs in those nights, and the dawns are the expected time of seeking forgiveness. Ibn ʿAmr al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "yastaghfirūn" means "yuṣallūn" (they pray). Al-Ḥasan said: they supplicate seeking forgiveness. The apparent meaning is that standing in the night and this right in wealth is among the recommended acts, and the greatest increase in reward comes from performing the recommended. Al-Qāḍī Mundhir ibn Saʿīd said: this right is the obligatory zakāh, and this was weakened on the ground that the sūrah is Meccan, and the obligation of zakāh was in Medina. It was said: it was obligatory and then abrogated, and this was weakened on the ground that God Most High did not legislate taking of wealth in Mecca before the Hijrah.

The sāʾil is the one who asks for charity, and the maḥrūm, linguistically, is the one prevented from something. ʿAlqamah said:

The one who feeds from the spoils on the day of spoils, his feeding is wherever he turns, and the deprived one remains deprived.

As for the verse, it is the one who is reckoned wealthy and so is deprived of charity because of his abstinence. It was also said: the one from whom the possibilities of provision are distant after being near, so that deprivation befalls him. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the maḥrūm is the one who has no share of wealth in Islam. Zayd ibn Aslam said: he is the one whose fruit has been destroyed by blight. It was said: the one whose livestock has died. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: he is the dog. It was said: the one whose wealth does not grow. It was said: the maḥrūf, the one who hardly ever earns. Other views were also said, and all these sayings are examples, not specifications, and what unites them is that he is the one who has no wealth due to a deprivation that befell him.

﴿And in the earth are signs﴾ that indicate the Maker, His power and His governance, in that it is like a carpet for what is above it, and in it are the mountain passes for travellers; and it is divided into plain and rugged, sea and land, and adjacent tracts of hard and soft, fertile and salt-marsh, and it is fertilized with kinds of plants; and in it are springs, minerals, and creatures scattered across its sea and land, differing in forms. Qatādah read: "āyatun," in the singular. (for those who have certainty): they are those who looked with sound reflection, and that led them to certainty in what the Messengers brought, so they became certain and no doubt entered them.

﴿And in yourselves﴾: at the beginning of their creation and their transition from state to state, and what He placed in the form of the human being of subtle senses, and what is arranged upon the intellect given to him of wondrous knowledge and strange crafts, and other things beyond counting.

﴿And in heaven is your provision﴾. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid, and Ibn Jubayr said: the rain and the snow, since it is the cause of sustenance, and every constant spring is from snow.
