Indeed, He is the Wise, the Knowing."﴾ ﴿[Abraham] said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people,﴾ ﴿to send upon them stones of clay,﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for the transgressors."﴾ ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers.﴾ ﴿But We found not in it except one house of the Muslims.﴾ ﴿And We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And in Moses [there is a sign], when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority.﴾ ﴿But he turned away with his supporters and said, "A magician or a madman."﴾ ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and threw them into the sea, while he was blameworthy.﴾ ﴿And in ʿAd [there is a sign], when We sent upon them the barren wind.﴾ ﴿It left nothing it came upon but that it reduced it to ruin.﴾ ﴿And in Thamud [there is a sign], when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time."﴾ ﴿But they defied the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were watching.﴾ ﴿And they were not able to stand [against it], nor were they among those who could defend themselves.﴾ ﴿And [We destroyed] the people of Noah before them. Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people.﴾

﴿Has there reached you﴾: It is a confirmation, so that the listener's attention is gathered, just as when you wish to tell someone a remarkable story, you first ask him whether he has heard of it or not, while you in fact expect him to say no. It also asks the listener to relate the story, and in it there is an exaltation of the account and an alert that it is not from the knowledge of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); rather, he knew it through revelation. The guest, whether one or many, is the same in this respect. He began with the story of Abraham (peace be upon him), although it came later than the story of ʿAd, to humble the Arabs, since he was their highest forefather, and because the messengers who visited him came to destroy the people of Lot, since they had denied him. Therefore, there is in it a warning and threat to the Arabs, an admonition and a lesson, and a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding what befalls him from his people. He described them as "the honoured" because of their honour with Allah, Exalted is He, like His saying about the angels: ﴿Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26]. This was said by al-Hasan. So it is a quality that was already theirs, or it was because of Abraham's honouring them, since he served them himself, along with his wife Sarah, and hastened to prepare hospitality for them. It was also said: it was because he raised their seats in a newly arisen manner. ʿIkrimah read "al-Mukarramin" with a shadda, and he applied the word "guest" to them because they were in the form of guests, as Abraham hosted them, or because he supposed them to be such. Their number was mentioned earlier in Surah Hud. The word ﴿idh﴾ (when) is governed by "the honoured" if the quality is one newly arisen through Abraham's action; otherwise it is governed by the sense of verbal action contained in "guest," or by an implied "remember." These are reported opinions. Al-Jumhur read ﴿qalu salaman﴾ with the accusative, as a verbal noun standing in place of its verb, which is dispensed with.

﴿Qala salamun﴾ with the nominative, where it is an omitted-predicate subject, its estimated sense being: "upon you is peace." He intended to answer them with something better than what they had greeted him with, adhering to the courtesy of Allah, Exalted is He, since "salaman" is a supplication. It is also permissible that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "my affair is peace," and "salamun" is a declarative sentence whose content has already been established and occurred. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is apt that "salaman" be governed by "qalu," on the basis that "salaman" is taken to mean "qawlan," and the meaning then is: they said a greeting, and a saying whose meaning is "salaman." This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Wathhab, al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn Jubayr and Talha read ﴿qala silmun﴾ with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam, and the meaning is: "we are peace," or "you are peace." Both were also read in the nominative. It was also read: ﴿salaman qalu silman﴾, with both in the accusative, and the second's sin with a kasra and its lam with a sukun.

﴿Qawmun munkarun﴾: Abu al-ʿAliyah said: he disliked their greeting in that land and at that time. It was also said: "We do not recognise them, and we have no familiarity with them." It was also said: this was his question, as if he said: "You are an unfamiliar people, so inform me who you are." "Qawmun" is the predicate of an omitted subject, which he estimated as "you," but what suits the state of Abraham (peace be upon him) is that he would not address them with that, since it contains the lack of intimacy that is not hidden. Rather, it appears that the estimate is: "These are an unfamiliar people." He said that to himself, or to those with him from his followers and servants, in a manner that the guests would not hear.

﴿Then he turned quickly to his family﴾: That is, he went away in the midst of his speech, concealing his departure, hastening. ﴿And brought a fat calf﴾: Among the courtesies of the host is to conceal his matter, and to hasten with the hospitality without the guest perceiving it, lest the guest prevent him from bringing the hospitality. That he joined ﴿fa-jaʾa﴾ (and came) to ﴿fa-raghā﴾ (turned quickly) indicates the speed of his bringing the hospitality, and that it was prepared in advance for whoever came to him. In Surah Hud he said: ﴿So he did not delay to bring a roasted calf﴾ [Hud: 69], and this also indicates that the calf was already roasted before their arrival. Qatadah said: most of his wealth was cattle. This indicates that he would bring for the guest more than he himself eats. Peace be upon him, he was generous to guests, and it suffices you that he endowed hospitality with endowments that nations maintain, despite the differences of their religions and races.

﴿He placed it before them﴾: In this is the courtesy of the host in bringing the hospitality close to the one who eats, and in it is the offering of food to eat, for in that there is encouragement to eat. This differs from one who serves food but does not urge its eating, for the present guest may suppose that he served it merely as a matter of formality, and so the guest may refrain from eating. This exists in the nature of some people, to the extent that when the guest insists and persists in eating, some of them take from the best of what has been brought and most excellent, and give it to his servant, with the intention of setting it aside for a later time that he himself will eat. It was also said: the hamza in ﴿a-lā﴾ (will you not) is interrogative of denial, and there seems to be an omitted element, estimated as: "they refrained from eating, so he denounced their abstention and said: ﴿Will you not eat?﴾" It is reported in a hadith: "Indeed they said, 'We do not eat except what we pay for.' He said to them, 'I do not permit it to you except for a price.' They said, 'And what is it?' He said, 'That you mention the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, at the beginning, and praise Him at the end of eating.' Then some of them said to others: 'Truly, Allah took him as a friend.'"

﴿And he felt apprehension of them﴾: That is, when they persisted in refraining from eating, he felt apprehension of them. This is because a guest's eating is a security and an indication of the ease of his mind, and food has a sanctity and an obligation, while refusing it is an estrangement. So Abraham (peace be upon him) feared that their refusal to eat his food was only because they intended some evil, so they said: "Fear not," and informed him that they were angels. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it came to his mind that they were angels sent for punishment. Their knowledge of what he concealed within himself of fear is only through Allah's informing His angels of what is in his soul, or through the appearance of its sign on his face, so they inferred the inward from that. It is reported from Yahya ibn Shaddad: Gabriel (peace be upon him) touched the calf with his wing, and it got up, running, until it caught up with its mother.

﴿A learned boy﴾: That is, he will be learned, and in this is good tidings of his life, so that he would be among the scholars. It is reported from al-Hasan: "a learned one" is a prophet. The majority hold that the one given good tidings of was Isaac, son of Sarah. Mujahid said: it was Ishmael. It was also said: he knew they were angels from the fact that they gave him tidings of the unseen, and the tidings came after reassurance and sitting. The tidings were of a male, because that is more gladdening to the soul and more delightful. He described him as "learned" because that is the quality by which the perfect human is distinguished, apart from beauty of form and strength.

﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry﴾: That is, toward her house. She had been in a corner, looking at them and listening to their speech. It was also said: ﴿fa-aqbalat﴾ means she began to shout. It was said: she found the heat of the blood and slapped her face out of shame. As for ﴿sarrah﴾ (a loud cry), Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Sufyan said it means a shriek. The poet said:

"We joined with the guiding [she-camels], and beyond it their [shrill] cries, in a loud cry that was not separated."

Qatadah and ʿIkrimah said it means a moan. It was said: she said "uhh!" with a cry and wonder. Ibn Bahr said: it means a group, that is, of women who rushed to look at the angels. Al-Jawhari said: the ṣarrah is a shriek, a group, and a severity.

﴿And struck her face﴾: That is, she slapped it. Ibn ʿAbbas said this, and it is also what one does when a matter that arrives surprises and amazes him, and it is the act of women when they are amazed at something. Al-Suddi and Sufyan said: she struck her forehead with her palm, and this is still practised among people to this day.

﴿And said, "[I am] an old barren woman"﴾: That is, the two conditions came together in her, that she was old, which prevents childbearing, and that she was barren, meaning one who has never borne a child at all. So how could I bear? She was amazed at this.

﴿They said, "Thus"﴾: That is, like the statement we have informed you of: ﴿"Thus has your Lord said."﴾ He is the One capable of bringing into being what is deemed unlikely. It is reported that Gabriel (peace be upon him) said to her: "Look at the ceiling of your house." She looked, and behold, its beams were budding and bearing fruit.

﴿Indeed, He is the Wise﴾: That is, possessing wisdom. ﴿The Knowing﴾ of what serves the interests.

When Abraham (peace be upon him) knew that they were angels, and that they do not descend except by the permission of Allah, Exalted is He, as messengers, he said: ﴿What is your business?﴾ up to ﴿a criminal people﴾: that is, people possessed of crimes, and these are the grave sins, such as disbelief and others.

﴿To send upon them﴾: That is, to destroy them with them, ﴿stones of clay﴾: and it is the sijjil, clay that is baked as bricks are baked until it becomes hard like stones. ﴿Marked﴾: that is, distinguished, with the name of its owner upon each one of them. It was also said: "marked" means that they are stones of punishment. It was also said: "marked" means that they are not of the stones of this world. ﴿For the transgressors﴾: and they are those who exceed the bound in disbelief.

﴿So We brought out whoever was in it﴾: in the town upon whose people the punishment descended.

﴿But not one house﴾: it is the house of Lot (peace be upon him), namely Lot and his two daughters only. It was also said: thirteen persons. Al-Rummani said: the verse indicates that faith is Islam, and al-Zamakhshari said the same, and both of them are Muʿtazilites.

﴿And We left in it﴾: that is, in the town, ﴿a sign﴾: a mark. Ibn Jurayj said: a very large stone, layered. It was also said: black, stinking water. It is permissible that "fīhā" (in it) refers to the destruction by which they were destroyed, for it is among the wonders of destruction, by making the upper parts of the town its lower parts and by raining down stones. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿And in Moses﴾ is conjoined to ﴿And We left in it﴾, that is: in the story of Moses. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿And in Moses﴾ is conjoined to ﴿And on the earth are signs for the certain﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 20]. But this is very far-fetched, and the Qur'an is too exalted for the like of it. Al-Zamakhshari also said: or it is conjoined to His saying ﴿And We left in it a sign﴾, in the sense of: "And We placed in Moses a sign," like the poet's saying:

"I fed her straw and cold water."

He ended. There is no need to supply "and We left" (wa-taraknā), because it is possible that the governing element of the genitive phrase is "wa-taraknā."

﴿So he turned away with his supporters﴾: that is, he turned aside and withdrew, as He said: ﴿and turned away with his side﴾ [Fussilat: 51]. It was also said: "with his strength and authority." Ibn Zayd said: "with his supporters" means with his whole body. Qatadah said: with his people.

﴿And said, "A magician or a madman"﴾: he supposed one of the two, or deliberately lied, while knowing that he was truly a messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Abu ʿUbaydah said: "aw" here means "wa" (and). This is indicated by the fact that Pharaoh said both: ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing magician﴾ [al-Araf: 109], and ﴿He said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 27]. Abu ʿUbaydah cited the verse of Jarir:

"Ath-laba al-fawaris, or Rabah, you equated them with Tuhayya and the stomachs (of the herd)."

Nor is there any necessity to take *aw* (أو) to mean *waw* (و), since the meaning would then be that he said both, and he left it vague to the listener; so *aw* is for indefiniteness. (هو مُلِيمٌ): that is, he had committed sins for which he deserved blame.

(العَقِيمَ) is the one in which there is no good. Among winds, it may be rain in winter, or the fertilizing of trees. In the Sahih it is reported: "I was given victory by the *saba* (east wind), and 'Ad was destroyed by the *dabur* (west wind)." So the view of those who said it is the *saba*, or the *janub* (south wind), or the *nakba*, which is a wind between two winds that veers away from the direction of the qiblah, and is therefore called *nakba*, is not sound, because it contradicts the established text from the Messenger ﷺ that it was the *dabur*.

﴿ما تَذَرُ مِن شَيْءٍ أتَتْ عَلَيْهِ﴾: This is a general statement that is specified (by context). Like His saying: ﴿تُدَمِّرُ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ بِأمْرِ رَبِّها﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25], that is, of what God willed to destroy and annihilate, whether people, dwellings, trees or plants, because God did not will for it to destroy the mountains, the hills, the rocks, or the world that was not of the people of 'Ad.

﴿إلّا جَعَلَتْهُ كالرَّمِيمِ﴾: This is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). *Al-Ramim* was already explained in (Surah) Ya-Sin. Here al-Suddi said it means dust; Qatadah said dry crushed herbage (al-hashim); Mujahid said decayed; Qutrub said ash; and Ibn 'Isa said that which is crushed and does not return to its former state, taking the *hamzah* in *aramma* to indicate negation. It is reported that the wind used to pass over the people, among whom was a man of the people of 'Ad, and it would snatch him from among them and destroy him.

﴿تَمَتَّعُوا حَتّى حِينٍ﴾: Al-Hasan said: this was when Salih was sent to them. They were commanded to believe in what he brought and to enjoy (life) until their terms came. Then they transgressed after that, and for this reason the conjunction *fa* (ف), which implies that the transgression came after what they were commanded, is used. So it corresponds literally and in actual occurrence. Al-Farra' said: this command to enjoy (life) came after the slaughter of the she-camel, and *al-hin* is the three days in which they were threatened with punishment at their completion. So the transgression had already occurred before they were told "enjoy yourselves." There is no necessity that compels one to accept al-Farra's view, since it is not in a sequential order in existence.

The majority (of reciters) read *al-sa'iqah* (الصّاعِقَةُ). 'Umar and 'Uthman, may God be pleased with them both, and al-Kisa'i read *al-sa'qah* (الصَّعْقَةُ), which here means the cry. Al-Hasan read *al-sa'iqah*, and Zayd ibn 'Ali (read) like the *qira'ah* (recitation) of al-Kisa'i.

﴿وهم يَنْظُرُونَ﴾: That is, suddenly, while they were looking with their eyes; this is what al-Tabari said, and it was during the day. Mujahid said: ﴿وهم يَنْظُرُونَ﴾ means they were waiting for that during those three days of which they were informed, and they saw its signs in their hearts; and the anticipation of punishment is more severe than the punishment itself.

﴿فَما اسْتَطاعُوا مِن قِيامٍ﴾: in accordance with His saying: ﴿فَأصْبَحُوا في دارِهِمْ جاثِمِينَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 78]. Negating the ability (*istita'ah*) is more emphatic than negating power (*qudrah*).

﴿وما كانُوا مُنْتَصِرِينَ﴾ is more emphatic than negating being helped: that is, they were not able to flee, nor were they among those who would defend themselves so as to repel what had befallen them. It was also said that *min qiyam* (مِن قِيامٍ) is from their saying: "what he does when he is unable to repel it," so the meaning is not the uprightness of the stature; this was said by Qatadah.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (وقَوْمِ) in the genitive, as a conjunction with what preceded, that is, "and in the (destruction of the) people of Nuh"; and this is the reading of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud). The remaining seven read it in the accusative, and Abu 'Amr in one narration also. It was said: it is conjoined to the pronoun in (*fa-akhadhatahum*); it was also said: it is conjoined to ﴿فَنَبَذْناهُمْ﴾, because the meaning of each of them is "so We destroyed them." It was also said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimated form is: "and We destroyed the people of Nuh," due to the meaning of the speech indicating it. It was also said: by an implied *udhkur* (اذْكُرْ, "remember"). 'Abd al-Warith, Mahbub and al-Asma'i related from Abu 'Amr, and Abu al-Sammal, and Ibn Miqsam (read): *wa-qawmu Nuhin* (وَقَوْمُ نُوحٍ) in the nominative, as an inchoative (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted, that is, "We destroyed them."

This is because a guest's eating is a security and an indication of the ease of his mind, and food has a sanctity and an obligation, while refusing it is an estrangement. So Abraham (peace be upon him) feared that their refusal to eat his food was only because they intended some evil, so they said: "Fear not," and informed him that they were angels. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it came to his mind that they were angels sent for punishment. Their knowledge of what he concealed within himself of fear is only through Allah's informing His angels of what is in his soul, or through the appearance of its sign on his face, so they inferred the inward from that. It is reported from Yahya ibn Shaddad: Gabriel (peace be upon him) touched the calf with his wing, and it got up, running, until it caught up with its mother.

﴿A learned boy﴾: That is, he will be learned, and in this is good tidings of his life, so that he would be among the scholars. It is reported from al-Hasan: "a learned one" is a prophet. The majority hold that the one given good tidings of was Isaac, son of Sarah. Mujahid said: it was Ishmael. It was also said: he knew they were angels from the fact that they gave him tidings of the unseen, and the tidings came after reassurance and sitting. The tidings were of a male, because that is more gladdening to the soul and more delightful. He described him as "learned" because that is the quality by which the perfect human is distinguished, apart from beauty of form and strength.

﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry﴾: That is, toward her house. She had been in a corner, looking at them and listening to their speech. It was also said: ﴿fa-aqbalat﴾ means she began to shout. It was said: she found the heat of the blood and slapped her face out of shame. As for ﴿sarrah﴾ (a loud cry), Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Sufyan said it means a shriek. The poet said:

"We joined with the guiding [she-camels], and beyond it their [shrill] cries, in a loud cry that was not separated."

Qatadah and ʿIkrimah said it means a moan. It was said: she said "uhh!" with a cry and wonder. Ibn Bahr said: it means a group, that is, of women who rushed to look at the angels. Al-Jawhari said: the ṣarrah is a shriek, a group, and a severity.

﴿And struck her face﴾: That is, she slapped it. Ibn ʿAbbas said this, and it is also what one does when a matter that arrives surprises and amazes him, and it is the act of women when they are amazed at something. Al-Suddi and Sufyan said: she struck her forehead with her palm, and this is still practised among people to this day.

﴿And said, "[I am] an old barren woman"﴾: That is, the two conditions came together in her, that she was old, which prevents childbearing, and that she was barren, meaning one who has never borne a child at all. So how could I bear? She was amazed at this.

﴿They said, "Thus"﴾: That is, like the statement we have informed you of: ﴿"Thus has your Lord said."﴾ He is the One capable of bringing into being what is deemed unlikely. It is reported that Gabriel (peace be upon him) said to her: "Look at the ceiling of your house." She looked, and behold, its beams were budding and bearing fruit.

﴿Indeed, He is the Wise﴾: That is, possessing wisdom. ﴿The Knowing﴾ of what serves the interests.

When Abraham (peace be upon him) knew that they were angels, and that they do not descend except by the permission of Allah, Exalted is He, as messengers, he said: ﴿What is your business?﴾ up to ﴿a criminal people﴾: that is, people possessed of crimes, and these are the grave sins, such as disbelief and others.

﴿To send upon them﴾: That is, to destroy them with them, ﴿stones of clay﴾: and it is the sijjil, clay that is baked as bricks are baked until it becomes hard like stones. ﴿Marked﴾: that is, distinguished, with the name of its owner upon each one of them. It was also said: "marked" means that they are stones of punishment. It was also said: "marked" means that they are not of the stones of this world. ﴿For the transgressors﴾: and they are those who exceed the bound in disbelief.

﴿So We brought out whoever was in it﴾: in the town upon whose people the punishment descended.

﴿But not one house﴾: it is the house of Lot (peace be upon him), namely Lot and his two daughters only. It was also said: thirteen persons. Al-Rummani said: the verse indicates that faith is Islam, and al-Zamakhshari said the same, and both of them are Muʿtazilites.

﴿And We left in it﴾: that is, in the town, ﴿a sign﴾: a mark. Ibn Jurayj said: a very large stone, layered. It was also said: black, stinking water. It is permissible that "fīhā" (in it) refers to the destruction by which they were destroyed, for it is among the wonders of destruction, by making the upper parts of the town its lower parts and by raining down stones. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿And in Moses﴾ is conjoined to ﴿And We left in it﴾, that is: in the story of Moses. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿And in Moses﴾ is conjoined to ﴿And on the earth are signs for the certain﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 20]. But this is very far-fetched, and the Qur'an is too exalted for the like of it. Al-Zamakhshari also said: or it is conjoined to His saying ﴿And We left in it a sign﴾, in the sense of: "And We placed in Moses a sign," like the poet's saying:

"I fed her straw and cold water."

He ended. There is no need to supply "and We left" (wa-taraknā), because it is possible that the governing element of the genitive phrase is "wa-taraknā."

﴿So he turned away with his supporters﴾: that is, he turned aside and withdrew, as He said: ﴿and turned away with his side﴾ [Fussilat: 51]. It was also said: "with his strength and authority." Ibn Zayd said: "with his supporters" means with his whole body. Qatadah said: with his people.

﴿And said, "A magician or a madman"﴾: he supposed one of the two, or deliberately lied, while knowing that he was truly a messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Abu ʿUbaydah said: "aw" here means "wa" (and). This is indicated by the fact that Pharaoh said both: ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing magician﴾ [al-Araf: 109], and ﴿He said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 27]. Abu ʿUbaydah cited the verse of Jarir:

"Ath-laba al-fawaris, or Rabah, you equated them with Tuhayya and the stomachs (of the herd)."

Nor is there any necessity to take *aw* (أو) to mean *waw* (و), since the meaning would then be that he said both, and he left it vague to the listener; so *aw* is for indefiniteness. (هو مُلِيمٌ): that is, he had committed sins for which he deserved blame.

(العَقِيمَ) is the one in which there is no good. Among winds, it may be rain in winter, or the fertilizing of trees. In the Sahih it is reported: "I was given victory by the *saba* (east wind), and 'Ad was destroyed by the *dabur* (west wind)." So the view of those who said it is the *saba*, or the *janub* (south wind), or the *nakba*, which is a wind between two winds that veers away from the direction of the qiblah, and is therefore called *nakba*, is not sound, because it contradicts the established text from the Messenger ﷺ that it was the *dabur*.

﴿ما تَذَرُ مِن شَيْءٍ أتَتْ عَلَيْهِ﴾: This is a general statement that is specified (by context). Like His saying: ﴿تُدَمِّرُ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ بِأمْرِ رَبِّها﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25], that is, of what God willed to destroy and annihilate, whether people, dwellings, trees or plants, because God did not will for it to destroy the mountains, the hills, the rocks, or the world that was not of the people of 'Ad.

﴿إلّا جَعَلَتْهُ كالرَّمِيمِ﴾: This is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). *Al-Ramim* was already explained in (Surah) Ya-Sin. Here al-Suddi said it means dust; Qatadah said dry crushed herbage (al-hashim); Mujahid said decayed; Qutrub said ash; and Ibn 'Isa said that which is crushed and does not return to its former state, taking the *hamzah* in *aramma* to indicate negation. It is reported that the wind used to pass over the people, among whom was a man of the people of 'Ad, and it would snatch him from among them and destroy him.

﴿تَمَتَّعُوا حَتّى حِينٍ﴾: Al-Hasan said: this was when Salih was sent to them. They were commanded to believe in what he brought and to enjoy (life) until their terms came. Then they transgressed after that, and for this reason the conjunction *fa* (ف), which implies that the transgression came after what they were commanded, is used. So it corresponds literally and in actual occurrence. Al-Farra' said: this command to enjoy (life) came after the slaughter of the she-camel, and *al-hin* is the three days in which they were threatened with punishment at their completion. So the transgression had already occurred before they were told "enjoy yourselves." There is no necessity that compels one to accept al-Farra's view, since it is not in a sequential order in existence.

The majority (of reciters) read *al-sa'iqah* (الصّاعِقَةُ). 'Umar and 'Uthman, may God be pleased with them both, and al-Kisa'i read *al-sa'qah* (الصَّعْقَةُ), which here means the cry. Al-Hasan read *al-sa'iqah*, and Zayd ibn 'Ali (read) like the *qira'ah* (recitation) of al-Kisa'i.

﴿وهم يَنْظُرُونَ﴾: That is, suddenly, while they were looking with their eyes; this is what al-Tabari said, and it was during the day. Mujahid said: ﴿وهم يَنْظُرُونَ﴾ means they were waiting for that during those three days of which they were informed, and they saw its signs in their hearts; and the anticipation of punishment is more severe than the punishment itself.

﴿فَما اسْتَطاعُوا مِن قِيامٍ﴾: in accordance with His saying: ﴿فَأصْبَحُوا في دارِهِمْ جاثِمِينَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 78]. Negating the ability (*istita'ah*) is more emphatic than negating power (*qudrah*).

﴿وما كانُوا مُنْتَصِرِينَ﴾ is more emphatic than negating being helped: that is, they were not able to flee, nor were they among those who would defend themselves so as to repel what had befallen them. It was also said that *min qiyam* (مِن قِيامٍ) is from their saying: "what he does when he is unable to repel it," so the meaning is not the uprightness of the stature; this was said by Qatadah.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (وقَوْمِ) in the genitive, as a conjunction with what preceded, that is, "and in the (destruction of the) people of Nuh"; and this is the reading of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud). The remaining seven read it in the accusative, and Abu 'Amr in one narration also. It was said: it is conjoined to the pronoun in (*fa-akhadhatahum*); it was also said: it is conjoined to ﴿فَنَبَذْناهُمْ﴾, because the meaning of each of them is "so We destroyed them." It was also said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimated form is: "and We destroyed the people of Nuh," due to the meaning of the speech indicating it. It was also said: by an implied *udhkur* (اذْكُرْ, "remember"). 'Abd al-Warith, Mahbub and al-Asma'i related from Abu 'Amr, and Abu al-Sammal, and Ibn Miqsam (read): *wa-qawmu Nuhin* (وَقَوْمُ نُوحٍ) in the nominative, as an inchoative (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted, that is, "We destroyed them."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 51, verses 24–46 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Has there reached you the story of Abraham's honoured guests?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Peace, [you are] an unfamiliar people."﴾ ﴿Then he turned quickly to his family and brought a fat calf.﴾ ﴿He placed it before them, [saying], "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿And he felt apprehension of them. They said, "Fear not," and gave him good tidings of a learned boy.﴾ ﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry, and she struck her face and said, "[I am] an old barren woman."﴾ ﴿They said, "Thus has your Lord said. Indeed, He is the Wise, the Knowing."﴾ ﴿[Abraham] said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people,﴾ ﴿to send upon them stones of clay,﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for the transgressors."﴾ ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers.﴾ ﴿But We found not in it except one house of the Muslims.﴾ ﴿And We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And in Moses [there is a sign], when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority.﴾ ﴿But he turned away with his supporters and said, "A magician or a madman."﴾ ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and threw them into the sea, while he was blameworthy.﴾ ﴿And in ʿAd [there is a sign], when We sent upon them the barren wind.﴾ ﴿It left nothing it came upon but that it reduced it to ruin.﴾ ﴿And in Thamud [there is a sign], when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time."﴾ ﴿But they defied the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were watching.﴾ ﴿And they were not able to stand [against it], nor were they among those who could defend themselves.﴾ ﴿And [We destroyed] the people of Noah before them. Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people.﴾

﴿Has there reached you﴾: It is a confirmation, so that the listener's attention is gathered, just as when you wish to tell someone a remarkable story, you first ask him whether he has heard of it or not, while you in fact expect him to say no. It also asks the listener to relate the story, and in it there is an exaltation of the account and an alert that it is not from the knowledge of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); rather, he knew it through revelation. The guest, whether one or many, is the same in this respect. He began with the story of Abraham (peace be upon him), although it came later than the story of ʿAd, to humble the Arabs, since he was their highest forefather, and because the messengers who visited him came to destroy the people of Lot, since they had denied him. Therefore, there is in it a warning and threat to the Arabs, an admonition and a lesson, and a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding what befalls him from his people. He described them as "the honoured" because of their honour with Allah, Exalted is He, like His saying about the angels: ﴿Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26]. This was said by al-Hasan. So it is a quality that was already theirs, or it was because of Abraham's honouring them, since he served them himself, along with his wife Sarah, and hastened to prepare hospitality for them. It was also said: it was because he raised their seats in a newly arisen manner. ʿIkrimah read "al-Mukarramin" with a shadda, and he applied the word "guest" to them because they were in the form of guests, as Abraham hosted them, or because he supposed them to be such. Their number was mentioned earlier in Surah Hud. The word ﴿idh﴾ (when) is governed by "the honoured" if the quality is one newly arisen through Abraham's action; otherwise it is governed by the sense of verbal action contained in "guest," or by an implied "remember." These are reported opinions. Al-Jumhur read ﴿qalu salaman﴾ with the accusative, as a verbal noun standing in place of its verb, which is dispensed with.

﴿Qala salamun﴾ with the nominative, where it is an omitted-predicate subject, its estimated sense being: "upon you is peace." He intended to answer them with something better than what they had greeted him with, adhering to the courtesy of Allah, Exalted is He, since "salaman" is a supplication. It is also permissible that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "my affair is peace," and "salamun" is a declarative sentence whose content has already been established and occurred. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is apt that "salaman" be governed by "qalu," on the basis that "salaman" is taken to mean "qawlan," and the meaning then is: they said a greeting, and a saying whose meaning is "salaman." This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Wathhab, al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn Jubayr and Talha read ﴿qala silmun﴾ with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam, and the meaning is: "we are peace," or "you are peace." Both were also read in the nominative. It was also read: ﴿salaman qalu silman﴾, with both in the accusative, and the second's sin with a kasra and its lam with a sukun.

﴿Qawmun munkarun﴾: Abu al-ʿAliyah said: he disliked their greeting in that land and at that time. It was also said: "We do not recognise them, and we have no familiarity with them." It was also said: this was his question, as if he said: "You are an unfamiliar people, so inform me who you are." "Qawmun" is the predicate of an omitted subject, which he estimated as "you," but what suits the state of Abraham (peace be upon him) is that he would not address them with that, since it contains the lack of intimacy that is not hidden. Rather, it appears that the estimate is: "These are an unfamiliar people." He said that to himself, or to those with him from his followers and servants, in a manner that the guests would not hear.

﴿Then he turned quickly to his family﴾: That is, he went away in the midst of his speech, concealing his departure, hastening. ﴿And brought a fat calf﴾: Among the courtesies of the host is to conceal his matter, and to hasten with the hospitality without the guest perceiving it, lest the guest prevent him from bringing the hospitality. That he joined ﴿fa-jaʾa﴾ (and came) to ﴿fa-raghā﴾ (turned quickly) indicates the speed of his bringing the hospitality, and that it was prepared in advance for whoever came to him. In Surah Hud he said: ﴿So he did not delay to bring a roasted calf﴾ [Hud: 69], and this also indicates that the calf was already roasted before their arrival. Qatadah said: most of his wealth was cattle. This indicates that he would bring for the guest more than he himself eats. Peace be upon him, he was generous to guests, and it suffices you that he endowed hospitality with endowments that nations maintain, despite the differences of their religions and races.

﴿He placed it before them﴾: In this is the courtesy of the host in bringing the hospitality close to the one who eats, and in it is the offering of food to eat, for in that there is encouragement to eat. This differs from one who serves food but does not urge its eating, for the present guest may suppose that he served it merely as a matter of formality, and so the guest may refrain from eating. This exists in the nature of some people, to the extent that when the guest insists and persists in eating, some of them take from the best of what has been brought and most excellent, and give it to his servant, with the intention of setting it aside for a later time that he himself will eat. It was also said: the hamza in ﴿a-lā﴾ (will you not) is interrogative of denial, and there seems to be an omitted element, estimated as: "they refrained from eating, so he denounced their abstention and said: ﴿Will you not eat?﴾" It is reported in a hadith: "Indeed they said, 'We do not eat except what we pay for.' ﴿ما تَذَرُ مِن شَيْءٍ أتَتْ عَلَيْهِ﴾: This is a general statement that is specified (by context). Like His saying: ﴿تُدَمِّرُ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ بِأمْرِ رَبِّها﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25], that is, of what God willed to destroy and annihilate, whether people, dwellings, trees or plants, because God did not will for it to destroy the mountains, the hills, the rocks, or the world that was not of the people of 'Ad.

﴿إلّا جَعَلَتْهُ كالرَّمِيمِ﴾: This is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). *Al-Ramim* was already explained in (Surah) Ya-Sin. Here al-Suddi said it means dust; Qatadah said dry crushed herbage (al-hashim); Mujahid said decayed; Qutrub said ash; and Ibn 'Isa said that which is crushed and does not return to its former state, taking the *hamzah* in *aramma* to indicate negation. It is reported that the wind used to pass over the people, among whom was a man of the people of 'Ad, and it would snatch him from among them and destroy him.

﴿تَمَتَّعُوا حَتّى حِينٍ﴾: Al-Hasan said: this was when Salih was sent to them. They were commanded to believe in what he brought and to enjoy (life) until their terms came. Then they transgressed after that, and for this reason the conjunction *fa* (ف), which implies that the transgression came after what they were commanded, is used. So it corresponds literally and in actual occurrence. Al-Farra' said: this command to enjoy (life) came after the slaughter of the she-camel, and *al-hin* is the three days in which they were threatened with punishment at their completion. So the transgression had already occurred before they were told "enjoy yourselves." There is no necessity that compels one to accept al-Farra's view, since it is not in a sequential order in existence.

The majority (of reciters) read *al-sa'iqah* (الصّاعِقَةُ). 'Umar and 'Uthman, may God be pleased with them both, and al-Kisa'i read *al-sa'qah* (الصَّعْقَةُ), which here means the cry. Al-Hasan read *al-sa'iqah*, and Zayd ibn 'Ali (read) like the *qira'ah* (recitation) of al-Kisa'i.

﴿وهم يَنْظُرُونَ﴾: That is, suddenly, while they were looking with their eyes; this is what al-Tabari said, and it was during the day. Mujahid said: ﴿وهم يَنْظُرُونَ﴾ means they were waiting for that during those three days of which they were informed, and they saw its signs in their hearts; and the anticipation of punishment is more severe than the punishment itself.

﴿فَما اسْتَطاعُوا مِن قِيامٍ﴾: in accordance with His saying: ﴿فَأصْبَحُوا في دارِهِمْ جاثِمِينَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 78]. Negating the ability (*istita'ah*) is more emphatic than negating power (*qudrah*).

﴿وما كانُوا مُنْتَصِرِينَ﴾ is more emphatic than negating being helped: that is, they were not able to flee, nor were they among those who would defend themselves so as to repel what had befallen them. It was also said that *min qiyam* (مِن قِيامٍ) is from their saying: "what he does when he is unable to repel it," so the meaning is not the uprightness of the stature; this was said by Qatadah.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (وقَوْمِ) in the genitive, as a conjunction with what preceded, that is, "and in the (destruction of the) people of Nuh"; and this is the reading of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud). The remaining seven read it in the accusative, and Abu 'Amr in one narration also. It was said: it is conjoined to the pronoun in (*fa-akhadhatahum*); it was also said: it is conjoined to ﴿فَنَبَذْناهُمْ﴾, because the meaning of each of them is "so We destroyed them." It was also said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimated form is: "and We destroyed the people of Nuh," due to the meaning of the speech indicating it. It was also said: by an implied *udhkur* (اذْكُرْ, "remember"). 'Abd al-Warith, Mahbub and al-Asma'i related from Abu 'Amr, and Abu al-Sammal, and Ibn Miqsam (read): *wa-qawmu Nuhin* (وَقَوْمُ نُوحٍ) in the nominative, as an inchoative (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted, that is, "We destroyed them."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 51, verses 24–46 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Has there reached you the story of Abraham's honoured guests?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Peace, [you are] an unfamiliar people."﴾ ﴿Then he turned quickly to his family and brought a fat calf.﴾ ﴿He placed it before them, [saying], "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿And he felt apprehension of them. They said, "Fear not," and gave him good tidings of a learned boy.﴾ ﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry, and she struck her face and said, "[I am] an old barren woman."﴾ ﴿They said, "Thus has your Lord said. Indeed, He is the Wise, the Knowing."﴾ ﴿[Abraham] said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people,﴾ ﴿to send upon them stones of clay,﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for the transgressors."﴾ ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers.﴾ ﴿But We found not in it except one house of the Muslims.﴾ ﴿And We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And in Moses [there is a sign], when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority.﴾ ﴿But he turned away with his supporters and said, "A magician or a madman."﴾ ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and threw them into the sea, while he was blameworthy.﴾ ﴿And in ʿAd [there is a sign], when We sent upon them the barren wind.﴾ ﴿It left nothing it came upon but that it reduced it to ruin.﴾ ﴿And in Thamud [there is a sign], when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time."﴾ ﴿But they defied the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were watching.﴾ ﴿And they were not able to stand [against it], nor were they among those who could defend themselves.﴾ ﴿And [We destroyed] the people of Noah before them. Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people.﴾

﴿Has there reached you﴾: It is a confirmation, so that the listener's attention is gathered, just as when you wish to tell someone a remarkable story, you first ask him whether he has heard of it or not, while you in fact expect him to say no. It also asks the listener to relate the story, and in it there is an exaltation of the account and an alert that it is not from the knowledge of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); rather, he knew it through revelation. The guest, whether one or many, is the same in this respect. He began with the story of Abraham (peace be upon him), although it came later than the story of ʿAd, to humble the Arabs, since he was their highest forefather, and because the messengers who visited him came to destroy the people of Lot, since they had denied him. Therefore, there is in it a warning and threat to the Arabs, an admonition and a lesson, and a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding what befalls him from his people. He described them as "the honoured" because of their honour with Allah, Exalted is He, like His saying about the angels: ﴿Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26]. This was said by al-Hasan. So it is a quality that was already theirs, or it was because of Abraham's honouring them, since he served them himself, along with his wife Sarah, and hastened to prepare hospitality for them. It was also said: it was because he raised their seats in a newly arisen manner. ʿIkrimah read "al-Mukarramin" with a shadda, and he applied the word "guest" to them because they were in the form of guests, as Abraham hosted them, or because he supposed them to be such. Their number was mentioned earlier in Surah Hud. The word ﴿idh﴾ (when) is governed by "the honoured" if the quality is one newly arisen through Abraham's action; otherwise it is governed by the sense of verbal action contained in "guest," or by an implied "remember." These are reported opinions. Al-Jumhur read ﴿qalu salaman﴾ with the accusative, as a verbal noun standing in place of its verb, which is dispensed with.

﴿Qala salamun﴾ with the nominative, where it is an omitted-predicate subject, its estimated sense being: "upon you is peace." He intended to answer them with something better than what they had greeted him with, adhering to the courtesy of Allah, Exalted is He, since "salaman" is a supplication. It is also permissible that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "my affair is peace," and "salamun" is a declarative sentence whose content has already been established and occurred. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is apt that "salaman" be governed by "qalu," on the basis that "salaman" is taken to mean "qawlan," and the meaning then is: they said a greeting, and a saying whose meaning is "salaman." This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Wathhab, al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn Jubayr and Talha read ﴿qala silmun﴾ with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam, and the meaning is: "we are peace," or "you are peace." Both were also read in the nominative. It was also read: ﴿salaman qalu silman﴾, with both in the accusative, and the second's sin with a kasra and its lam with a sukun.

﴿Qawmun munkarun﴾: Abu al-ʿAliyah said: he disliked their greeting in that land and at that time. It was also said: "We do not recognise them, and we have no familiarity with them." It was also said: this was his question, as if he said: "You are an unfamiliar people, so inform me who you are." "Qawmun" is the predicate of an omitted subject, which he estimated as "you," but what suits the state of Abraham (peace be upon him) is that he would not address them with that, since it contains the lack of intimacy that is not hidden. Rather, it appears that the estimate is: "These are an unfamiliar people." He said that to himself, or to those with him from his followers and servants, in a manner that the guests would not hear.

﴿Then he turned quickly to his family﴾: That is, he went away in the midst of his speech, concealing his departure, hastening. ﴿And brought a fat calf﴾: Among the courtesies of the host is to conceal his matter, and to hasten with the hospitality without the guest perceiving it, lest the guest prevent him from bringing the hospitality. That he joined ﴿fa-jaʾa﴾ (and came) to ﴿fa-raghā﴾ (turned quickly) indicates the speed of his bringing the hospitality, and that it was prepared in advance for whoever came to him. In Surah Hud he said: ﴿So he did not delay to bring a roasted calf﴾ [Hud: 69], and this also indicates that the calf was already roasted before their arrival. Qatadah said: most of his wealth was cattle. This indicates that he would bring for the guest more than he himself eats. Peace be upon him, he was generous to guests, and it suffices you that he endowed hospitality with endowments that nations maintain, despite the differences of their religions and races.

﴿He placed it before them﴾: In this is the courtesy of the host in bringing the hospitality close to the one who eats, and in it is the offering of food to eat, for in that there is encouragement to eat. This differs from one who serves food but does not urge its eating, for the present guest may suppose that he served it merely as a matter of formality, and so the guest may refrain from eating. This exists in the nature of some people, to the extent that when the guest insists and persists in eating, some of them take from the best of what has been brought and most excellent, and give it to his servant, with the intention of setting it aside for a later time that he himself will eat. It was also said: the hamza in ﴿a-lā﴾ (will you not) is interrogative of denial, and there seems to be an omitted element, estimated as: "they refrained from eating, so he denounced their abstention and said: ﴿Will you not eat?﴾" It is reported in a hadith: "Indeed they said, 'We do not eat except what we pay for.' He said to them, 'I do not permit it to you except for a price.' They said, 'And what is it?' He said, 'That you mention the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, at the beginning, and praise Him at the end of eating.' Then some of them said to others: 'Truly, Allah took him as a friend.'"

﴿And he felt apprehension of them﴾: That is, when they persisted in refraining from eating, he felt apprehension of them. This is because a guest's eating is a security and an indication of the ease of his mind, and food has a sanctity and an obligation, while refusing it is an estrangement. So Abraham (peace be upon him) feared that their refusal to eat his food was only because they intended some evil, so they said: "Fear not," and informed him that they were angels. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it came to his mind that they were angels sent for punishment. Their knowledge of what he concealed within himself of fear is only through Allah's informing His angels of what is in his soul, or through the appearance of its sign on his face, so they inferred the inward from that. It is reported from Yahya ibn Shaddad: Gabriel (peace be upon him) touched the calf with his wing, and it got up, running, until it caught up with its mother.

﴿A learned boy﴾: That is, he will be learned, and in this is good tidings of his life, so that he would be among the scholars. It is reported from al-Hasan: "a learned one" is a prophet. The majority hold that the one given good tidings of was Isaac, son of Sarah. Mujahid said: it was Ishmael. It was also said: he knew they were angels from the fact that they gave him tidings of the unseen, and the tidings came after reassurance and sitting. The tidings were of a male, because that is more gladdening to the soul and more delightful. He described him as "learned" because that is the quality by which the perfect human is distinguished, apart from beauty of form and strength.

﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry﴾: That is, toward her house. She had been in a corner, looking at them and listening to their speech. It was also said: ﴿fa-aqbalat﴾ means she began to shout. It was said: she found the heat of the blood and slapped her face out of shame. As for ﴿sarrah﴾ (a loud cry), Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Sufyan said it means a shriek. The poet said:

"We joined with the guiding [she-camels], and beyond it their [shrill] cries, in a loud cry that was not separated."

Qatadah and ʿIkrimah said it means a moan. It was said: she said "uhh!" with a cry and wonder. Ibn Bahr said: it means a group, that is, of women who rushed to look at the angels. Al-Jawhari said: the ṣarrah is a shriek, a group, and a severity.

﴿And struck her face﴾: That is, she slapped it. Ibn ʿAbbas said this, and it is also what one does when a matter that arrives surprises and amazes him, and it is the act of women when they are amazed at something. Al-Suddi and Sufyan said: she struck her forehead with her palm, and this is still practised among people to this day.

﴿And said, "[I am] an old barren woman"﴾: That is, the two conditions came together in her, that she was old, which prevents childbearing, and that she was barren, meaning one who has never borne a child at all. So how could I bear? She was amazed at this.

﴿They said, "Thus"﴾: That is, like the statement we have informed you of: ﴿"Thus has your Lord said."﴾ He is the One capable of bringing into being what is deemed unlikely. It is reported that Gabriel (peace be upon him) said to her: "Look at the ceiling of your house." She looked, and behold, its beams were budding and bearing fruit.

﴿Indeed, He is the Wise﴾: That is, possessing wisdom. ﴿The Knowing﴾ of what serves the interests.

When Abraham (peace be upon him) knew that they were angels, and that they do not descend except by the permission of Allah, Exalted is He, as messengers, he said: ﴿What is your business?﴾ up to ﴿a criminal people﴾: that is, people possessed of crimes, and these are the grave sins, such as disbelief and others.

﴿To send upon them﴾: That is, to destroy them with them, ﴿stones of clay﴾: and it is the sijjil, clay that is baked as bricks are baked until it becomes hard like stones. ﴿Marked﴾: that is, distinguished, with the name of its owner upon each one of them. It was also said: "marked" means that they are stones of punishment. It was also said: "marked" means that they are not of the stones of this world. ﴿For the transgressors﴾: and they are those who exceed the bound in disbelief.

﴿So We brought out whoever was in it﴾: in the town upon whose people the punishment descended.

﴿But not one house﴾: it is the house of Lot (peace be upon him), namely Lot and his two daughters only. It was also said: thirteen persons. Al-Rummani said: the verse indicates that faith is Islam, and al-Zamakhshari said the same, and both of them are Muʿtazilites.

﴿And We left in it﴾: that is, in the town, ﴿a sign﴾: a mark. Ibn Jurayj said: a very large stone, layered. It was also said: black, stinking water. It is permissible that "fīhā" (in it) refers to the destruction by which they were destroyed, for it is among the wonders of destruction, by making the upper parts of the town its lower parts and by raining down stones. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿And in Moses﴾ is conjoined to ﴿And We left in it﴾, that is: in the story of Moses. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿And in Moses﴾ is conjoined to ﴿And on the earth are signs for the certain﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 20]. But this is very far-fetched, and the Qur'an is too exalted for the like of it. Al-Zamakhshari also said: or it is conjoined to His saying ﴿And We left in it a sign﴾, in the sense of: "And We placed in Moses a sign," like the poet's saying:

"I fed her straw and cold water."

He ended. There is no need to supply "and We left" (wa-taraknā), because it is possible that the governing element of the genitive phrase is "wa-taraknā."

﴿So he turned away with his supporters﴾: that is, he turned aside and withdrew, as He said: ﴿and turned away with his side﴾ [Fussilat: 51]. It was also said: "with his strength and authority." Ibn Zayd said: "with his supporters" means with his whole body. Qatadah said: with his people.

﴿And said, "A magician or a madman"﴾: he supposed one of the two, or deliberately lied, while knowing that he was truly a messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Abu ʿUbaydah said: "aw" here means "wa" (and). This is indicated by the fact that Pharaoh said both: ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing magician﴾ [al-Araf: 109], and ﴿He said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 27]. Abu ʿUbaydah cited the verse of Jarir:

"Ath-laba al-fawaris, or Rabah, you equated them with Tuhayya and the stomachs (of the herd)."

Nor is there any necessity to take *aw* (أو) to mean *waw* (و), since the meaning would then be that he said both, and he left it vague to the listener; so *aw* is for indefiniteness. (هو مُلِيمٌ): that is, he had committed sins for which he deserved blame.

(العَقِيمَ) is the one in which there is no good. Among winds, it may be rain in winter, or the fertilizing of trees. In the Sahih it is reported: "I was given victory by the *saba* (east wind), and 'Ad was destroyed by the *dabur* (west wind)." (p-142) That is, "And We built the heaven." It is an instance of *al-ishtighal* (a verb governing an object that is pronominalised by a suffix, so the noun is put in the accusative by an implied verb). The same applies to "And We spread out the earth." Abu al-Sammal, Mujahid and Ibn Miqsam read *al-sama'* and *al-ard* in the nominative, as a *mubtada'* (grammatical subject beginning a nominal sentence). "With *ayd*" means "with strength." This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah, and it is like His saying ﴿Dawud, the possessor of strength﴾ [Sad: 17].

﴿And indeed We are expanding it﴾: that is, expanding its building. The clause is a *hal* (circumstantial clause), meaning "We built it while expanding it," like the saying "Zayd came, and he is hastening," meaning "hastening." The heaven is such that the earth, and the water and air surrounding it, are like a point in the middle of a circle. Ibn Zayd said something close to this, namely that *al-wus* (expansion) refers to the heaven. It has also been said that *lamusi'un* means "powerful and capable," that is, "truly capable," from *al-wus*, which means capacity. Al-Hasan said: He expanded the provision by means of rain and water.

﴿So how excellent are the spreaders﴾, and ﴿We created pairs﴾: Mujahid said that this refers to opposites and counterparts, such as night and day, misery and happiness, guidance and misguidance, heaven and earth, blackness and whiteness, health and sickness, disbelief and faith, and the like. Al-Tabari preferred this view, arguing that it is more indicative of the power that brings opposites into existence, unlike things that act by their nature, such as heating and cooling. Al-Hasan gave examples of some of the things mentioned earlier and said: Every two of them is a pair, while God, the Exalted, is singular, having no like. Ibn Zayd and others said: *(from every thing)* means from among the animals, *﴿We created pairs﴾*: male and female. It has also been said that the intended meaning of *thing* is the genus, and that what falls under a genus consists of two kinds. Thus from every genus He created two kinds of substances, such as the growing and the inert. From the growing come the perceiving and the plant, and from the perceiving come the speaking and the mute. All of this indicates that He is one, with no multiplicity in Him.

*(So that you may remember)*: that is, that I am the builder of the heaven, the spreader of the earth, and the creator of the pairs, exalted above having a partner. It has also been said that *lamusi'un* means "powerful and capable," that is, "truly capable," from *al-wus*, which means capacity. Al-Hasan said: He expanded the provision by means of rain and water.

﴿So how excellent are the spreaders﴾, and ﴿We created pairs﴾: Mujahid said that this refers to opposites and counterparts, such as night and day, misery and happiness, guidance and misguidance, heaven and earth, blackness and whiteness, health and sickness, disbelief and faith, and the like. Al-Tabari preferred this view, arguing that it is more indicative of the power that brings opposites into existence, unlike things that act by their nature, such as heating and cooling. Al-Hasan gave examples of some of the things mentioned earlier and said: Every two of them is a pair, while God, the Exalted, is singular, having no like. Ibn Zayd and others said: *(from every thing)* means from among the animals, *﴿We created pairs﴾*: male and female. It has also been said that the intended meaning of *thing* is the genus, and that what falls under a genus consists of two kinds. Thus from every genus He created two kinds of substances, such as the growing and the inert. From the growing come the perceiving and the plant, and from the perceiving come the speaking and the mute. All of this indicates that He is one, with no multiplicity in Him.

*(So that you may remember)*: that is, that I am the builder of the heaven, the spreader of the earth, and the creator of the pairs, exalted above having a partner. Or, you may remember that He is not incapable of resurrecting bodies and gathering spirits. Ubayy read *tatadhakkarun* with two *ta*'s and a light *dhal*. It has also been said that it means "in order that you may remember, and so recognise the Creator and worship Him."

﴿So flee to God﴾: this is a command to enter into faith and obedience to God. The command to do this was phrased with the word *flight*, to alert that behind people lie punishment, chastisement and a matter from which one ought to flee. Thus the word *fafirru* combines warning and summons. This meaning is reflected in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no refuge and no escape from You except to You," as Ibn Atiyyah said, and it is a fine interpretation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "To His obedience and reward, away from His disobedience and punishment. Affirm His oneness and do not associate anything with Him." He repeated ﴿Indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner﴾ at the command to obey and the prohibition of associating partners, so that it would be known that faith does not benefit except together with action, just as action does not benefit except together with faith, and that no one succeeds before God except the one who combines both. Do you not see His saying: ﴿The soul will not benefit from its faith if it had not believed before, or had not earned good through its faith﴾ [al-An'am: 158]? The meaning is: "Say, O Muhammad, so flee to God." End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah. We have already refuted him in the commentary on ﴿The soul will not benefit from its faith﴾ [al-An'am: 158], in its proper place.

*(Thus)*: that is, the matter of the earlier nations when messengers came to them is like the matter of the disbelievers to whom you were sent, namely denial.

﴿A sorcerer or a madman﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 39]: *aw* here is for division, meaning that some said "sorcerer," some said "madman," and some said both. Do you not see that the people of Noah, peace be upon him, did not say of him that he was a sorcerer, but rather said "there is madness in him"? Thus they gathered in the pronoun, and *aw* indicates division.

﴿Did they charge one another with it?﴾: that is, with that statement. This is a rebuke and an expression of wonder at the convergence of the disbelievers' minds on denying the prophets despite the separation of their times. ﴿Rather, they are a transgressing people﴾: that is, they did not charge one another with it, because they did not live in one time. Rather, one cause united them, namely that they were tyrants. They were dominant on earth, corrupting in it, and overbearing.

﴿So turn away from them﴾: that is, turn away from those to whom you repeatedly conveyed the message, (p-143) and who did not respond.

﴿And you are not blameworthy﴾: since you have conveyed the message and given counsel.

﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾: it has an effect on them and on whomever God has decreed will believe. What the apparent meaning indicates of conciliation (*muwada'ah*) has been abrogated (*mansukh*) by the verse of the sword (*ayat al-sayf*). It is reported from Ali, may God honour his face, that when ﴿So turn away from them﴾ was revealed, the Muslims were saddened and thought it was a command to turn away from everyone and that revelation had ceased. Then ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾ was revealed, and they rejoiced at that.

﴿Except that they worship Me﴾: that is, ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind﴾ except the obedient, as said by Zayd ibn Aslam and Sufyan. This is supported by the report of Ibn Abbas from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "And I did not create the jinn and humankind except the believers among them." Ali and Ibn Abbas said: ﴿except that they worship Me﴾: except to command them to worship Me, and that they acknowledge worship to Me. He expressed it as *liya'buduni* (that they worship Me), since worship is contained in the command. On this view, "jinn and humankind" is general. It has also been said that the meaning may be: "except as those prepared to worship Me." It is as if the verse enumerates His blessings: I created for them senses, minds and bodies inclined toward worship, just as you say: "This is created for such-and-such," even if what it was created for does not come from it, just as you say: "The pen is sharpened for writing with," and it may or may not be used for writing. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Except for the sake of worship, and I did not intend from all of them except that." If you say: "If He intended worship from them, they would all be worshippers." I say: He intended that they worship Him by choice, not by compulsion, because He created them with the capacity to do so. Some of them chose to abandon worship, though He wanted it. Had He wanted it by force and compulsion, it would have come from all of them. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah. Mujahid said: ﴿except that they worship Me﴾: that they know Me (*liya'rifuni*). Ibn Zayd said: to make them, in worship, subject to wretchedness and happiness. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "except for worship," and he said that this is the apparent meaning of the wording. It has been said: "except that they abase themselves before My decree." Al-Kalbi said: "except that they affirm My oneness (*liyuwahhidunI*)," so the believer affirms His oneness in hardship and ease, while the disbeliever does so only in hardship. Ikrimah said: "that they obey Me," so that I reward the worshipper and punish the denier. Mujahid also said: "except for commanding and forbidding."

﴿I do not want any provision from them﴾: that is, that they should provide for themselves or for others.

﴿Nor do I want them to feed Me﴾: that is, that they should feed My creation. It is therefore an elision of a noun (*hadhf mudaf*), and the attribution to the pronoun is permissible, as said by Ibn Abbas. It has also been said: ﴿that they feed Me﴾ means "that they benefit Me," so He mentioned a part of the benefits and made it indicate the whole. Al-Zamakhshari said: He means that His relationship with His servants is not like the relationship of masters with their slaves, because slave-owners only own them so that they may help them obtain their livelihoods and provisions. Either a slave is equipped for trade, seeking profit, or is assigned to farming to till the land, or is hired in a craft to benefit from his wage, or is a firewood gatherer, a grass cutter, a water carrier, a cook, a baker, or other such workers and professions employed in the means of subsistence and the doors of sustenance. But the Owner of owners says to them: "Busy yourselves with what makes you happy in yourselves. I do not want to employ you in obtaining My provision or your provision, for I am rich without you and your services, and I bestow upon you your provision and what sets you right and sustains you from Me. There is none but Me alone." End of quotation. This is exaggeration and rhetorical flourish. Ibn Muhaysin read *al-Razzaq* (the Provider) as an active participle, as he read ﴿and in the heaven﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22]. Humayd also read it so. Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read ﴿the Possessor of strength, the Firm﴾ in the genitive, as an attribute of *al-quwwah* (strength) in the sense of power, as al-Zamakhshari said, or as if He had said *dhu al-ayd*. Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) allowed that it be an attribute of *dhu*, and it is genitive by attraction (*khafd 'ala al-jiwar*), like the saying: "This is the hole of a worn-out lizard."

﴿For those who did wrong, indeed they will have a share (*dhanuban*) like the share of their companions﴾: they are the people of Mecca and others among the disbelievers who denied the Messenger (ﷺ). *Dhanub* means a portion or share. ﴿Like the share of their companions﴾: from the earlier nations who denied the messengers, in destruction and punishment. It is reported from Qatadah: a bucketful of God's punishment, like the bucketful of their companions. Al-Jawhari said: *dhanub* is a bucket full of water, and it is not called *dhanub* when it is empty; its plural is *'adad*, and in the sense of plenty it is *dhana'ib*. *Dhanub* is also a horse with a long tail, and *dhanub* is a share, and *dhanub* is meat at the lower part of the back. Ibn al-A'rabi said: one says "a *yawm dhanub*," meaning a day of long evil that does not end.

﴿So woe to those who disbelieved, from their day which they are promised﴾: it has been said that this is the day of Badr. It has also been said (p-144) that it is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Which they are promised﴾: that is, the day with which they are threatened, or which they are promised.
